title: 13 Best Agent Gateways in 2026 for MCP, A2A and LLM Traffic: Kong, Bifrost, AgentCore, Arcade
abstract: Agents no longer just call a model. They call tools over MCP, delegate to other agents over A2A, and act inside business systems. The best agent gateways sit on that path and decide who can do what. This list compares 13 of them on traffic coverage, identity, deployment and price. An agent gateway is a control point that authenticates agents, filters the tools they see, and logs every call. A plain LLM gateway only routes model requests. An agent gateway adds MCP tool governance, agent identity and, increasingly, A2A traffic control. Our ranking below is editorial and weighs 5 criteria: traffic coverage, identity and authorization, deployment options, maturity, and price transparency. Kong governs LLM, MCP and A2A traffic from 1 control plane. Version 2.0 moved AI features into first-class Providers, Models, MCP Servers and Agents entities . Bifrost is an Apache 2.0 Go gateway covering models, MCP tools and A2A agents in 1 deployment. Maxim reports 10,000+ models across 25+ providers. Its benchmark claims 11 µs mean overhead at 5,000 RPS . Gravitee runs an LLM Proxy, MCP Proxy and A2A Proxy on 1 runtime. All 3 share 1 authentication, policy and OpenTelemetry chain. The A2A Proxy supports RFC 8693 token exchange and skill-level authorization. AgentCore Gateway gives agents 1 managed endpoint for tools, models and other agents . It adds semantic tool search, Cedar policies and on-behalf-of token exchange. Pricing starts at $0.005 per 1,000 invocations . Arcade is an actions runtime, not a model router. Per Arcade , it checks the overlap of user and agent permissions on every action. Credentials never reach the LLM. It lists 8,000+ agent-optimized tools. Palo Alto Networks completed its Portkey acquisition in May 2026. The gateway reached GA inside Prisma AIRS in July 2026. Palo Alto describes it as a unified LLM, MCP and A2A gateway with 1 enforcement point. It runs in SaaS and hybrid models . Microsoft’s AI gateway extends API Management to model APIs, MCP servers and A2A agent APIs. It can expose REST APIs as MCP servers and front existing MCP servers. Agent Gateway is the network entry and exit point for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It assigns each agent a SPIFFE ID and can apply Model Armor to prompts and responses. Maxim lists up to 5,000 governed resources per gateway. ContextForge is an Apache 2.0 registry and proxy that federates MCP, REST, gRPC and A2A. It exposes agents as MCP tools and, per Maxim , deploys via Helm. Envoy AI Gateway became Agent Router and joined the Agentic AI Foundation in September 2026. It offers an OpenAI-compatible API plus an MCP gateway on Envoy. Composio is an MCP gateway and SaaS integration layer with managed OAuth and per-user connected accounts. Arcade lists a free tier of 100,000 tool calls per month and Pro from $29. TrueFoundry combines an LLM Gateway and centralized MCP access with training and deployment tooling. Pro costs $25 per user per month , with 20,000 requests and tool calls per user. Obot is an open-source platform bundling an MCP Gateway, LLM Gateway and device monitoring. It supports per-user auth, OAuth token exchange and audit logs. Start with traffic. If agents only call models, an LLM gateway is enough. If they call tools, you need MCP governance. If they delegate to other agents, check A2A support carefully. Then check identity. Ask whether user and agent permissions are enforced separately at execution time. Finally, check where it must run: single cloud, your VPC, or air-gapped. title: Perplexity Launches Orchestrator API for Failover and Model Routing
abstract: Perplexity has launched the Perplexity Orchestrator API , a single endpoint for frontier and open-weight models. It picks a serving provider by availability, capacity and latency , and bills everything through 1 account. Developers get fewer integrations and 1 invoice. The Perplexity Orchestrator API is a hosted inference gateway that serves many models behind 1 base URL. It covers frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI . It also serves open-weight models such as GLM, Kimi and DeepSeek, hosted by Perplexity or inference partners. It accepts OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages requests. Most teams only change the API key and base URL. The OpenAI base URL is https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1 . Anthropic SDK users point at https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator , without /v1 . Perplexity runs the same layer internally, across 85+ models and more than a dozen providers. Failover keeps the model fixed and swaps the deployment. A Claude request that fails on Anthropic can be served by AWS Bedrock instead. The reliability docs set these rules: You cannot pick a deployment yourself. Perplexity measured production traffic from October 4 to November 2, 2026. Claude and GPT requests through Perplexity succeeded more often than requests to any single provider measured. Daily success rates also varied less during provider incidents. The post gives no percentage success rates. Speed varied by provider too. For Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic was fastest on 15 of 30 days, AWS Bedrock on 15. Azure’s median output speed for GPT-5.6 Sol was 27% higher than OpenAI’s. Speed-aware routing is still in progress. Routing is in preview. You set model to perplexity/auto and pass a routing object. It holds a default_model and 1 to 5 routes , each with a name, description and model. A decision model reads the conversation and route descriptions. It never sees route names or model IDs. If nothing matches, or the decision model fails or times out, the default model answers. So do media inputs. Response headers report the result: x-perplexity-autoroute-outcome , -route and -confidence . The default policy sends traffic to GPT-6.1 Sol, with simple requests going to GPT-6 Luna. Perplexity also lists built-in Lower cost, Balanced and Higher quality profiles, plus an Auto effort preview. Perplexity tested this on a 63-task subset of Terminal-Bench 4.1 , run in Claude Code. Anthropic documents that Claude Fable 5.2 safeguards can block benign security and life sciences work. The routes covered security , biology and after_refusal requests. That is +3 tasks, at a higher estimated cost per task. Perplexity calls it an adjusted comparison; results vary by workload. Each request is billed at the answering model’s published per-token rate. Failover to another provider does not change the rate. Perplexity says there is no additional platform fee on top of credits . For example, perplexity/glm-5.3 lists $1.4 input, $4.4 output and $0.26 cache read per 1M tokens . Usage draws from prepaid Perplexity API credits, also purchasable through AWS Marketplace. Access is tiered by cumulative credit purchases : Check out the launch post , technical blog , quickstart , model catalog and routing docs . title: Not If, But How: Responding to Security Incidents in the Age of AI Attackers
abstract: Attackers now have powerful AI on their side. AI agents can scan, plan and run intrusions at machine speed, and they improve every month. The result is more attacks, more often and at global scale. In that environment, more companies will face a security incident at some point. What separates them is how they respond. Machine-speed threats call for a modern playbook with 4 pillars. Detect and contain automatically. Communicate fast and securely. Eradicate thoroughly. Keep shrinking the blast radius. This article shows the trend through 6 months of incidents. It then looks at a few companies, with Fireworks AI as a model of mature, structurally sound response. AI has changed the economics of attacking. Tasks that took skilled people days can now be delegated to agents. In November, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said AI misuse had reached a “critical inflection point” . They report that attackers use AI to shorten timelines and run multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. CrowdStrike reported that 1 group used AI agents against more than 200 organizations in 11 days . Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 found attacks moving about 4 times faster than a year earlier. The shift started earlier. In 2025, Anthropic disrupted a campaign where AI did 80 to 90% of tactical work with little human input. The tools keep improving, so the pace will keep rising. AI infrastructure is an especially attractive target, because AI access itself has value. The last 6 months show what that looks like. Incidents appeared across every layer of the AI stack. Together they show how broad the activity has become. May: package registries. On May 10 and 11, the “Mini Shai-Hulud” campaign altered about 170 npm packages and some PyPI libraries . Affected projects included AI SDKs from Mistral AI and Guardrails AI. The NHS cyber alert lists the specific versions to avoid. June: SaaS integrations. Klue, a market intelligence platform, disclosed misuse of OAuth tokens it held for customers. See case study 2. August: self-hosted AI gateways. Microsoft described intrusions into exposed, unpatched LiteLLM, RAGFlow and Kestra deployments. Fixed versions exist for all 3 tools . CISA had listed the LiteLLM flaw as known exploited on June 8. September: evaluation environments. Anthropic’s September threat report described attempts to obtain AI keys through software vendors. The Cloud Security Alliance summarized it . In 1 case, instructions were injected into a vendor’s automated evaluation sandbox. October and early November: developer platforms. At least 9 AI developer and hosting platforms disclosed incidents involving stored customer secrets in October. Wiz’s tracker later listed further disclosures, for 16 platforms in total. A tampered LiteLLM release, version 1.107.0, was also identified , and users were told to roll back. November: shared web vendors. On November 16, an attacker abused a flaw in Optimizely’s account signup flow to inject code into customer projects, reaching 178 organizations’ websites, according to Report URI, including HSBC, Salesforce, the BBC and Ledger. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses and skimmed payment forms; Optimizely removed the payload and fixed the flaw. Hudson Rock traced similar code through three other web services, beginning November 13. It is the same concentration pattern, one layer below the AI stack. Selected incidents: Dates follow the linked sources, which sometimes differ by a day. Several October entries rely on compilations by Wiz and Helix rather than primary vendor disclosures. There was no single vulnerability. According to the Cloud Security Alliance, entry points varied . The common target was stored environment variables, often holding AI provider API keys. AI keys carry real value, which explains the interest. CSA, citing Anthropic, notes that a key can be resold, used for compute or used as cover . Wiz estimated that misuse of 2 keys from these incidents exceeded $100,000 at list price . That is why spending caps matter. Concentration is the other shared factor. A platform that stores secrets for many customers naturally draws attention. CSA describes this as the platform-chain pattern . No company can promise it will never be breached. Every company can control how it responds. Against attackers that move at machine speed, that response rests on 4 pillars. 1. Detect and contain automatically: A human-speed shutdown is no longer enough. An AI-driven intruder can move between systems in minutes. Mature teams wire detection directly to containment. That means kill-switches, automatic token revocation and host isolation. Wiz recommends alerting on bulk secret reads , the clearest signal in this year’s incidents. The best setups act on that signal automatically. 2. Communicate fast, and securely: Speed still matters most for revocation. Customers need to rotate keys, and upstream providers need to revoke access at the source. CSA notes that deleting a key from a platform does not revoke it . Mature teams also choose the channel with care. A Five Eyes joint advisory warns against communicating over the network under investigation . It advises out-of-band communication instead. CISA’s playbooks likewise call for out-of-band communications infrastructure as part of preparation. That keeps an attacker who is still watching from learning the response plan. 3. Eradicate thoroughly: Closing the hole that was used is only the first step. Top teams assume the attacker planted backdoors and hunt for them. They bring in independent forensic experts, such as Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 or Mandiant. The same advisory recommends third-party incident response support . It also warns against fixing symptoms instead of the root cause. 4. Keep improving by shrinking the blast radius: Attackers improve every month, so security is never finished. The strongest proactive defense limits what any future attacker can reach. Zero Trust access means no credential is trusted by default. Ephemeral architecture means sensitive data is not kept at all. If data isn’t stored, it can’t be stolen. Some companies already apply these pillars. The 2 case studies below show how: Fireworks AI is an inference and training platform. It disclosed an incident in October, 2026, during a busy month for the industry. Its response is a strong example of mature, structurally sound incident response across the 4 pillars. Fireworks identified unauthorized use of internal credentials on October 6 . A second event began on October 24, through a third-party cloud provider that hosted its R&D machines. Fireworks detected that activity and closed it on the same day it began. That is the kind of operational agility machine-speed threats demand. Fireworks began notifying affected customers on October 7 , about 1 day after detection . It published a public bulletin on October 9 and has updated it as findings came in. It also notified law enforcement. The bulletin lists affected resource metadata and billing information. For certain customers, it also lists datasets, incomplete model weights and secrets. Pillar 3: eradicate thoroughly Fireworks engaged Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for forensic analysis. Bringing in an independent, top-tier team is a mature decision. It means the investigation looks beyond the first entry point, for anything an attacker may have left behind. Fireworks also completed rotation of employee API keys by October 9 . Pillar 4: a smaller blast radius by design Fireworks’ most important protection was already in place. It says it detected no impact to its Inference, Training SDK and Nexus products. All 3 run with zero data retention by default, so prompts and outputs are not stored at rest. That architecture kept the core products out of the reported impact. Fireworks has since gone further. It paused its Batch API , and its documentation says stored Batch inputs and outputs will be permanently deleted.

title: Google DeepMind Releases Gemini 4 Neon: 1M Context, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index
abstract: Google DeepMind just released Gemini 4 Neon . Gemini 4 Neon is a reasoning model that sits between Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It targets coding agents, knowledge work and science workflows. The developer pitch is near-frontier scores at a lower cost per task. Pricing is $3 per 1M input tokens and $15 per 1M output tokens. Neon is the middle model in the Gemini 4 family. Carbon handles the hardest long-horizon projects. Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution. Neon balances depth and efficiency between the two. As per the model card , Neon is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon. Google does not disclose parameter count or architecture. Inputs cover text, images, audio and video. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. Neon exposes multiple thinking levels. High is the default. xhigh is reserved for the hardest engineering, analytical and science workloads. For long agent runs, Neon supports context compaction and makes fewer redundant file reads. In Google Antigravity , Neon can act as an orchestrator. It directs parallel Gemini 4 Hydrogen subagents on smaller subtasks. Google compares Neon against Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol. All scores below are reported by Google, not independently reproduced. Neon does not win every row. Opus 5.5 leads Terminal-bench 4.1 (65.8% vs 65.2%) and FrontierCode 2.0 (47.3% vs 46.2%). GPT-6.2 Sol leads Chartography (75.1% vs 73.5%). On the Vals Index , Neon scores 70.9% and ranks #2. On the Agent Arena index it also ranks #2, with a score of 1336. Neon lists at $3 input, $0.15 cached input and $15 output per 1M tokens. Google says Neon at high thinking costs 32% less per task than Carbon. It also claims 50% to 80% lower cost per task vs rivals on Vals Index and Agent Arena. At xhigh, Google cites 36%+ lower cost than rivals at their highest settings. Those are per-task claims, not per-token prices. GPT-6.2 Sol lists at $2/$10. Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4/$20. Gemini 4 Carbon is $2/$10 until November 30, then $4/$20. Neon runs on the Gemini 4 safety and security stack . Google reports a 0.09% misaligned action rate on its agentic safety suite. It passes 99.2% of the agent honesty evaluation. It shows a 0.0% attack success rate on Gray Swan’s prompt injection benchmark at the highest thinking level. Its 2.45% shortcut rate on a coding cheating test is the lowest of any Gemini 4 model. *Scores from Google’s launch comparison table , self-reported. AA scores for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol match Artificial Analysis . Check out the launch post and the model card . title: Nutrient Data Extraction API: JSON Matching Your Schema With Per-Field Citations and Confidence
abstract: An LLM presents you a wrong value extracted from a document as fact. That error is costly, especially when basing decisions on it. The Nutrient Data Extraction API targets that problem. It parses PDFs, scans, images and Office files into spatial JSON or Markdown. Extract maps fields from a document onto your JSON schema, and split, classify and form endpoints provide useful primitives for your document pipelines. Each extracted value is anchored to a page via a bounding box, a match label and a confidence score. Nutrient (formerly PSPDFKit) runs the same engine behind an MCP server , agent skill, Mac app and SDK . Studio is Nutrient’s browser workspace for configuring and testing the API before integrating it in your application. It enables you to test parsing, extraction, classification , splitting, and form filling on your own files. A typical loop: Processors saved in Studio can then be called from the API by ID. Auto routes each page to structure , understand or agentic . If the mode is omitted, the API defaults to understand . * WholeDoc Bench parsing score, 5 November 2026; not extraction accuracy. Extract adds $0.006 per page. **API docs list text-mode extract; the agent skill starts at structure. Pricing is in dollars, from 1 balance shared across Nutrient’s cloud APIs, so teams can mix and match. The free plan gives you $5 monthly usage that covers about 330 understand-mode extractions. Starter costs $75 a month for $90 of usage; Growth costs $275 for $345. In Nutrient’s confidence post , a field scored 0.97 but came from the wrong column. The current score is a composite of optional signals: token probability, candidate margin, grounding and format. Nutrient’s NLI grounding model is open under Apache-2.0. A grounded value can still answer the wrong field. When no score exists, confidence is omitted, not low. Each field also gets a match label: id_match, id_match_multiblock, id_match_partial, fuzzy_match or not_found. Gate on the label first, then confidence. This demo covers flat schemas only; production needs type and business-rule checks. The 0.97 bar mirrors money fields in Nutrient’s mortgage tutorial . A document decision model powers classify and split . Nutrient reports 96.2% split F1 against 63.7% for Typesafe AI’s Jev. The hosted MCP server needs no API key. Claude Code connects with 1 command: Claude and Codex also work via OAuth. Default agentic mode costs $0.018 per page to parse. Coding agents can install the document-extraction-api skill with npx skills add pspdfkit-labs/nutrient-skills –skill document-extraction-api. On the Mac app, documents stay local only with a local model. Fully offline production needs the SDK . Nutrient’s new WholeDoc Bench scores whole documents, not single pages: 480 documents, 30+ languages, 7 areas. Selected rows, WholeDoc leaderboard , 5 November 2026, list prices. *Score still under review. Cross-page continuity is the biggest gap. On 44 documents with page-spanning tables, 15 of 19 settings rarely kept them whole. Nutrient built and ran it, and the main test set is private. The code is Apache-2.0, with a 10-document public sample. See the Data Extraction API , benchmarks , MCP server and agent skill on GitHub . Thanks to the Nutrient AI team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored . The post Nutrient Data Extraction API: JSON Matching Your Schema With Per-Field Citations and Confidence appeared first on MarkTechPost .

title: What I Learned From Kaggle + Google’s Free Agentic AI Course
abstract: What I Learned From Kaggle + Google’s Free Agentic AI Course Learn to build AI agents with Gemini and Google’s ADK through this free course, covering tools, memory, evaluation, and deployment. By Bala Priya C , KDnuggets Contributing Editor & Technical Content Specialist on November 19, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence I took the 5-Day AI Agents Intensive Course from Kaggle and Google . The course originally ran live from November 10 to 14, 2025, and is now available as a free, self-paced course on Kaggle. You can work through the whitepapers, hands-on codelabs, podcasts, and recorded livestreams at your own pace, exploring how AI agents work and what it takes to build them. A single prompt and a single response are easy to reason about. An agent adds a loop around that: the model picks an action, calls a tool, reads what came back, and decides what to do next. The loop brings questions that a one-shot call never raises. How does the agent remember the last turn, how do you know it picked the right tool, and what changes when it has to run somewhere other than your notebook? The course works through those questions. Each day pairs a whitepaper with two hands-on notebooks built on Gemini and the Agent Development Kit (ADK) , Google's open-source framework for building agents. You need Python and some experience calling a large language model API, but no prior knowledge of agents. These are my notes on what stood out. This article covers: How to tell when a task needs an agent, and the patterns for wiring several together How tools and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) connect agents to the outside world How sessions and memory give an agent the context it needs How to measure agent quality, and what it takes to run agents beyond a notebook Check out the course at this link: 5-Day AI Agents Intensive Course with Google | Kaggle Building a First Agent and Wiring Several Together The first day introduces agents and the architectures you can build with ADK. The first notebook, From Prompt to Action , builds a first agent, and the second, Agent Architectures , moves on to systems where several agents work together. In ADK, an agent is a small bundle: a name, a model, a description that other agents can read, instructions that set its behavior, and a list of tools. A runner executes it. An in-memory runner is fine for experiments, and anything real needs a persistent one. When one agent carries too many jobs, you split the work across several. The course covers a few ways to wire them together: a parent agent that chooses which sub-agent to call, a sequential pipeline, parallel branches that run at the same time, and a loop that repeats until a condition is met. In a sequential pipeline, each agent hands its output to the next. I'd reach for the pipeline first. It runs in a fixed order, so a failure points at one stage, and a model choosing between sub-agents needs tracing before you know what happened. Notebooks: From Prompt to Action and Agent Architectures Giving Agents Tools Tools are what let an agent do anything beyond writing text. The course covers four kinds. Built-in tools like Google Search come with the model. Function tools wrap your own Python functions. Agent tools let one agent hand a subtask to another while keeping control of the conversation. MCP tools connect to outside services through the protocol , so you skip writing a custom client for each one. The model decides how to call a function tool from its description alone. That is why the best-practices notebook spends its time on docstrings, type hints, and structured return values: the clearer the description, the fewer wrong calls. The course also covers human approval for long-running operations, where the agent pauses and waits for a person to confirm before it continues. My rule of thumb: when an agent picks the wrong tool, read the tool description before you touch the prompt. Notebooks: Agent Tools and Agent Tools Best Practices Adding Memory Across Turns and Sessions A model keeps nothing between calls. On every turn the agent has to send the conversation history again, and that history costs tokens. Memory in ADK splits into two parts. Short-term memory is the session , the conversation history, managed by a session service. Long-term memory is outside the session and is searched through a memory service, so facts can survive into the next conversation. The memory service comes in different forms. The in-memory version searches by keyword, and managed services can search by meaning. As a session grows, context compaction and caching keep both the cost and the context size under control. This brings us to effective context engineering , which means choosing what goes into the model's context on each turn. Retrieval from long-term memory comes in two modes. In reactive retrieval, the agent searches memory when it decides to. In proactive retrieval, the system searches before every turn and hands the agent the results. Proactive retrieval costs a search per turn and gives the agent relevant memories without asking. Reactive retrieval saves that cost and depends on the agent knowing when to look. Notebooks: Agent Sessions and Agent Memory Understanding Agent Quality and Evaluation Agents are non-deterministic: the same input can take a different path on the next run. A final spot check cannot cover that, so the course treats quality as part of the design from the start. Agent quality rests on two practices. Observability records what happened through logs, traces, and metrics. A trace shows each step the agent took, which makes a wrong answer debuggable after the fact. Evaluation scores two things: the final response, and the process behind it, such as which tools the agent called and in what order. Running evaluation continuously catches regressions early. Scoring the process matters because a correct answer can hide a bad path. An agent that calls the right tool three times when once was enough returns the same answer and costs three times as much. Notebooks: Agent Observability and Agent Evaluation Taking an Agent Beyond the Notebook The last day covers what happens after the demo works. Agents built by different teams, in different frameworks and languages, need a shared way to talk to each other. The Agent2Agent protocol provides one: an agent is exposed as a service, and other agents find out what it can do by reading its agent card. On the deployment side, the course puts an agent on a managed runtime, Vertex AI Agent Engine, and introduces CI/CD and AgentOps practices for keeping agents running after launch. It also mentions that ADK is available for Go and Java as well as Python. The course closes with an optional capstone project, where you build an agent of your own from the pieces above. Notebooks: Agent2Agent Communication and Agent Deployment Wrapping Up The course covers how to build an agent, how to give it tools and memory, how to measure it, and how to deploy it. The notebooks cover implementation with Google's ADK, and the whitepapers are good companion reads. In effect, you should be measuring both the path an agent takes and the answer it returns. Some resources for further learning: 5-Day AI Agents Intensive course guide Agent Development Kit (ADK) documentation Agent2Agent protocol Happy learning! Bala Priya is a developer, educator, and technical writer based in India. She writes about programming, data science, machine learning, and AI, with a focus on making complex technical ideas practical and approachable. She creates tutorials, how-to guides, and deep dives that help developers build, solve problems, and understand complex technical concepts. Her technical interests include LLM applications, agentic AI, graph algorithms, computer vision, explainable AI, and ML systems. When she’s not writing or coding, Bala is usually reading classic literature, epic fantasy, or speculative fiction.

title: One Table, Many Engines: Running BigQuery, Spark, and Trino on a Single Iceberg Copy
abstract: One Table, Many Engines: Running BigQuery, Spark, and Trino on a Single Iceberg Copy Run BigQuery, Apache Spark, and Trino on one Apache Iceberg table in Google Cloud's Lakehouse runtime catalog, with no copies or sync jobs, and see how Iceberg handles concurrent commits between engines. By KDnuggets on November 19, 2026 in Data Engineering In Partnership with Google Cloud Here is a common data engineering setup: BigQuery for analytics, Apache Spark for pipelines, and Trino for ad hoc questions that land on a Friday afternoon. Each engine gets its own copy of the data, while sync jobs do their best to keep this data aligned. Despite best efforts, data doesn't always stay consistent, and the lag between syncs inevitably becomes an issue. Consider a scenario where BigQuery says that an order status is shipped , while the Spark copy reports paid and awaiting shipment . No one can trust either until the next sync job finishes. Even if it eventually does finish, you're still paying for compute time to perform the sync and storage for multiple copies. And if it doesn't finish? You pay for engineering time to trace and fix the pipeline issues. Google Cloud's borderless Lakehouse and the Apache Iceberg open table format work together to help solve this. Every engine can read the same Parquet files and the same metadata layout without having to create separate copies. A shared catalog and commit protocol ensure that the engines agree on where the current version of the table lives, and on how a change gets committed without one writer trampling another. To test it out, I built a project of my own: one orders table, one Cloud Storage bucket registered once in the Lakehouse runtime catalog . Apache Spark creates and loads the table, Trino appends to it, and BigQuery updates and merges rows in place. Then I made Spark and Trino write at the same moment, on purpose, to see what Iceberg does when two commits collide. Figure 1. The project architecture. I ran every command here in a fresh Google Cloud project, and I've reported the outputs as they came back. You can find the full set of scripts in this repository . Architecture Overview: One Bucket, One Catalog, Three Engines The mental model is small. Every data file and every metadata file for the table sits in one Cloud Storage location. The catalog doesn't hold any data. Instead, it holds one thing of great importance: a pointer to each table's current version via its metadata.json file. Change the pointer, and you've changed the table. Spark and Trino reach the Lakehouse runtime catalog through the standard Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint ( https://biglake.googleapis.com/iceberg/v1/restcatalog ). BigQuery doesn't need any connector setup. It reads the same table with a four-part name: project.catalog.namespace.table For this guide, the four-part name is: my-project.one_table_catalog.shop.orders This is referred to as the P.C.N.T. naming convention , for Project.Catalog.Namespace.Table, which parallels BigQuery dataset syntax. The last design choice is who can access the bucket. The catalog supports two credential modes: Mode Who needs bucket access What the engine gets End-user credentials Every user and every job service account Nothing extra; each caller uses its own identity against Cloud Storage Credential vending mode Only the catalog's own service account A short-lived token scoped to the paths of the table being read or written I went with credential vending mode . With three engines and their service accounts in play, I'd rather grant bucket access to exactly one identity and manage everything else through catalog roles. Step 1: Creating the Catalog and the Bucket The bucket comes first. After that, the catalog is a single gcloud command. export PROJECT_ID="my-project" export REGION="us-central1" export BUCKET_NAME="${PROJECT_ID}-one-table-lakehouse" export CATALOG_ID="one_table_catalog" gcloud storage buckets create gs://${BUCKET_NAME} \ --project=${PROJECT_ID} \ --location=${REGION} \ --uniform-bucket-level-access gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs create ${CATALOG_ID} \ --project=${PROJECT_ID} \ --catalog-type=biglake \ --default-location=gs://${BUCKET_NAME} \ --credential-mode=vended-credentials The flag to watch is --catalog-type=biglake . That gives you a multiple-bucket catalog, whose name doesn't have to match a bucket and which can grow to more storage paths later. The catalog gets its own service account. With credential vending mode, it's the only identity that needs to touch the bucket: CATALOG_SA=$(gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs describe ${CATALOG_ID} \ --project=${PROJECT_ID} \ --format='value(biglake-service-account)') gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://${BUCKET_NAME} \ --member="serviceAccount:${CATALOG_SA}" \ --role="roles/storage.objectUser" That service account is created asynchronously, so the grant can fail if you run it immediately after its creation. If so, wait 20 seconds and run it again. The repo's script retries on its own. The describe output for my project came back with credential-mode: CREDENTIAL_MODE_VENDED_CREDENTIALS and catalog-type: CATALOG_TYPE_BIGLAKE . In your project, you can check both to verify. Figure 2. Project catalog details. Step 2: Creating and Loading the Table from Managed Service for Apache Spark Spark is up first because I am using it to create the table, and the table's write settings need to exist from the first commit. Changing write modes on a table that other engines already write to is how you end up with a mix of file layouts you didn't plan for. One cluster runs both engines. Trino is an optional component on the same Managed Service for Apache Spark cluster: gcloud dataproc clusters create one-table-cluster \ --project=${PROJECT_ID} --region=${REGION} --zone=${REGION}-a \ --image-version=2.3-debian12 \ --optional-components=ICEBERG,TRINO \ --enable-component-gateway \ --master-machine-type=n2-standard-4 --worker-machine-type=n2-standard-4 \ --num-workers=2 \ --properties="dataproc:dataproc.lakehouse.catalog.${CATALOG_ID}=projects/${PROJECT_ID}/catalogs/${CATALOG_ID}" The cluster's default service account needs the following roles on the project: roles/dataproc.worker roles/biglake.editor roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer The cluster requires nothing on the bucket, because the catalog vends it a token. That dataproc.lakehouse.catalog property wires Spark to the catalog in one line. It sets Spark's warehouse to gs://<bucket> . On older 2.3 image builds, it sets Spark warehouse to gs://BUCKET . With the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint, a gs:// warehouse URI addresses a single-bucket catalog named after the bucket, so my first Spark run wrote the table into a single-bucket catalog that Lakehouse had quietly created, and BigQuery could not find it under my multiple-bucket catalog. A multiple-bucket catalog is addressed as bl://projects/PROJECT_ID/catalogs/CATALOG_ID . It was a quick fix to the warehouse on the master node once the cluster was up: gcloud compute ssh one-table-cluster-m --zone=${REGION}-a --command="sudo sed -i \ 's#^spark.sql.catalog.${CATALOG_ID}.warehouse=.*#spark.sql.catalog.${CATALOG_ID}.warehouse=bl://projects/${PROJECT_ID}/catalogs/${CATALOG_ID}#' \ /etc/spark/conf/spark-defaults.conf" If gcloud biglake iceberg catalogs list shows a catalog of type CATALOG_TYPE_GCS_BUCKET that you never created, this is why. Now the table. Spark SQL, submitted as a job: CREATE NAMESPACE IF NOT EXISTS one_table_catalog.shop; CREATE TABLE one_table_catalog.shop.orders ( order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT, status STRING, amount DECIMAL(10,2), updated_at TIMESTAMP ) USING iceberg TBLPROPERTIES ( 'format-version' = '2', 'write.delete.mode' = 'copy-on-write', 'write.update.mode' = 'copy-on-write', 'write.merge.mode' = 'copy-on-write', 'gcp.biglake.bigquery-dml.enabled' = 'true' ); INSERT INTO one_table_catalog.shop.orders VALUES (1001, 501, 'pending', 49.99, TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 09:15:00'), (1002, 502, 'paid', 120.

title: Reducing Rollout Bottlenecks in Reinforcement Learning with NVIDIA Dynamo
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) uses rewards to train models to solve problems and complete tasks more successfully. Inference drives this process. Workers generate rollouts: sequences of model outputs, actions, and environment interactions. The RL framework scores the results, updates model weights, and sends those weights back to the workers for the next round. As RL training scales, redundant compute work, slow rollouts, weight updates, and worker failures can waste GPU capacity and delay training. NVIDIA Dynamo provides the serving layer to address these constraints, helping teams generate more accepted training samples and complete training iterations faster. This blog post explains the rollout bottlenecks that slow RL training and how Dynamo addresses them through routing, ModelExpress weight updates, and recovery. Figure 1. The RL loop generates rollouts, assigns rewards, and updates model weights before repeating 1. Why RL needs distributed rollout infrastructure A reasoning rollout may contain one response. A coding-agent rollout can involve repository exploration, edits, tool calls, and tests. These differences create an uneven workload across inference workers. Three constraints determine how effectively that workload supports training. Rollout completion time. When training requires a group of samples, the slowest required rollout can delay the next step. Distributing request counts evenly across GPUs does not necessarily distribute work evenly. Repeated context. Multiple attempts often begin with identical instructions, task descriptions, or coding repository context. Recomputing those prefixes consumes GPU capacity before new output is generated. Weight freshness. Training produces new model weights throughout the run. Workers must receive them according to the algorithm’s requirements for sampling and acceptable staleness. Addressing these constraints can let teams complete more iterations within a fixed compute budget. The right optimization depends on which constraint limits the workload. Figure 2. The three constraints on RL training: slow rollouts, redundant prompt processing, and timely weight updates 2. The Dynamo architecture for RL Dynamo sits between rollout orchestration and inference workers. The RL framework submits generation requests; Dynamo routes them to eligible capacity; inference engines execute the model. Figure 3. Dynamo coordinates rollout serving, the RL framework controls training and ModelExpress distributes weights The responsibilities of each component remain explicit: Component Role RL framework Optimization, rewards, environments, checkpoints, and sample acceptance Dynamo Routing, worker management, serving controls, and telemetry Inference engine Generation and application of updated weights ModelExpress Model-weight and artifact distribution through supported integrations Table 1. Component responsibilities in the Dynamo RL training loop The generation and weight administration follow distinct paths. Requests use the shared serving frontend, while refresh operations target selected workers under framework control. This lets the framework determine when workers may generate samples and which results are eligible for training. The separation allows teams to improve serving without transferring ownership of the learning process. Routing decisions determine where generation runs; the framework determines whether the resulting samples satisfy its training requirements. See the RL integration reference . 3. How Dynamo accelerates routing, weight distribution, and recovery KV-aware routing: Reduce repeated prompt computation RL often generates several solutions to the same task using a shared prompt. Sending these requests to a worker that has cached the prompt avoids repeated processing, saving GPU compute. But sending every request to that worker can create a queue, delaying rollouts and the next training step. Dynamo’s router balances KV cache reuse and worker load to reduce redundant computation and waiting. The objective is earlier completion of the samples needed for training. Figure 4. Dynamo balances cache reuse and worker load to reduce rollout delays ModelExpress: Reduce recurring weight-distribution overhead RL training repeatedly updates the model. Sending a full checkpoint to every rollout worker takes time and can interrupt generation. ModelExpress reduces this overhead by reusing weights already available in the cluster instead of loading from remote storage. Compatible workers can copy weights directly from another GPU over NIXL. Figure 5. ModelExpress loads weights from a running worker’s GPU memory, making them available sooner than loading from storage Delta weight transfer reduces the data sent between updates. Instead of moving the full model, it sends a compressed representation of what changed. Workers reconstruct the new weights from the matching base version, reducing transfer time and network traffic. This also helps recovery. A replacement worker can load a checkpoint and apply subsequent deltas to catch up with the training run. Healthy workers can continue generating rollouts while capacity is restored. Figure 6. ModelExpress accelerates weight updates by transferring compressed changes instead of the full model The RL framework coordinates when workers apply updates, handles cached state, and checks readiness before accepting new samples. Recovery: Limit the impact of worker failures Long training runs must accommodate worker failures without unnecessarily interrupting healthy capacity. Dynamo detects worker loss, directs new requests toward eligible workers and adds replacement workers to routing once ready, keeping rollout generation moving when a worker fails. Supported configurations also enable migration for eligible in-flight requests and graceful draining. The RL framework handles interrupted samples and ensures replacements use the required weights. Figure 7. Dynamo reroutes supported sessions to healthy workers, using saved history to avoid restarting the full rollout Dynamo in RL workflows Dynamo adoption in RL spans frontier-model development, managed infrastructure and open source frameworks: Microsoft AI used NVIDIA Dynamo to support RL rollout inference during post-training . CoreWeave uses Dynamo and ModelExpress to accelerate model weight updates by up to 15×. Cognition used Dynamo to manage inference workers and route rollouts during the post-training of SWE-1.7 . Prime Intellect uses Dynamo for distributed inference orchestration . H Company used Dynamo and ModelExpress to reduce average training-step time by up to 20% and GPU-hours by up to 5%. Open-source integrations connect Dynamo to existing RL stacks, including verl , NeMo RL , Slime , and prime-rl . Get started with Dynamo for RL Efficient RL infrastructure keeps rollout generation, weight distribution, and worker recovery moving together. Dynamo brings these serving capabilities into the training loop, helping teams turn distributed GPU capacity into accepted training samples and faster iterations. Explore the Dynamo RL documentation and start scaling the inference behind your next model. Acknowledgments Aichen Feng, Biswa Ranjan Panda, Elaine Hou, Hyunjae Woo, Jinyan Chen, John Thomson, Sean Choi, Sophia Yang, William Arnold, and Zhongdongming Dai contributed to this post.

title: Enabling Real-Time AI for Scientific Instruments with GPU-Native Data Acquisition
abstract: In science and industry, analyzing sensor measurements in real time can enable AI to adjust processes, guide experiments, and search for better operating conditions. Yet limits on how quickly the measured data can be moved and processed often shape how an instrument is designed, from readout electronics to acquisition timing. What could scientific instrument makers simplify—or make possible—if processing could keep pace with their sensors? NVIDIA DAQIRI is a software-defined data acquisition library that moves high-bandwidth instrument and sensor data into GPU-ready workflows. It enables developers to process measurements during acquisition without first writing them to disk. An NVIDIA Holoscan platform library, DAQIRI bridges sensors optimized for measurement with programmable GPU platforms for scientific analysis, AI inference, and feedback applications. For existing Ethernet-capable instruments, this opens opportunities to add processing and feedback capabilities, as described in the previous post, Enable Real-Time AI for High-Speed Data Acquisition with NVIDIA DAQIRI . For new instruments, it allows opportunities for reconsidering acquisition constraints from the start. This post explores how a new electron microscopy camera and GPU processing enable analysis during acquisition. It then introduces new DAQIRI features, including hardware packet reordering, performance and throughput improvements in the library, and a low-latency NIC polling mode for time-sensitive packet processing. Case study: Connecting high-dynamic-range imaging to GPU processing A high-dynamic-range electron microscopy camera developed at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s Molecular Foundry illustrates what becomes possible when advanced detectors and GPU processing are designed to work together. Electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS) measures the energy electrons lose as they interact with a sample, helping scientists identify which elements are present and how they are bonded together. These measurements contain both strong and faint signals. To capture those differences in intensity, the conventional approach uses two separately optimized acquisition processes in rapid succession. This requires precise coordination of the electron optics, exposure timing, and detector readout. The resulting measurements then need to be aligned and combined, adding complexity to both acquisition and processing. The new high-dynamic-range camera developed at the Molecular Foundry captures strong and faint signals together. This advancement simplifies the experimental setup and microscope optics, but generates more than 500 gigabits of data per second (Gbps)—a stream that must be received and processed to make those measurements useful during acquisition. This is over 500x faster than conventional EELS data streams, which greatly enhances the raw detector information available for further processing and analysis. Figure 1. Researchers at Berkeley Lab’s Molecular Foundry examine a hardware component beside the electron microscope used in the GPU-accelerated EELS workflow. Photo credit: Marilyn Sargent/Berkeley Lab Handling that stream requires an acquisition and processing pipeline designed to keep pace with the camera. This is where the collaboration between Berkeley Lab and NVIDIA brings together the camera, DAQIRI, and GPU-accelerated processing. FPGA readout electronics transmit detector data over Ethernet, DAQIRI receives the packets directly into GPU memory, and GPU processing assembles and corrects detector frames before reducing them to energy-loss spectra. Computation also improves the spatial information recovered from the detector, enabling submicron spatial resolution from sensor pixels measuring 5 micrometers across. Through this pipeline, the team enables inspection of the data during the measurement and adjusting the acquisition parameters and regions of interest in real time, all while processing high bandwidth data incoming at more than 500 Gbps. Figure 2. The workflow of the EELS measurement at Berkeley Lab sends the data directly into the GPU memory, from which GPU applications can process the data while the experiment is ongoing The benefits of this approach extend beyond electron microscopy. Connecting sensors to GPU processing can extract more information from measurements and give instrument makers greater flexibility in how they acquire, analyze, and act on data. Realizing those benefits requires efficient data movement, ordered payloads ready for processing, and low-latency communication for feedback. Designing acquisition paths for intelligent instruments The latest DAQIRI release adds hardware packet reordering, an optimized library backend for improved throughput, and direct polling for low-latency packet transmission and reception. Reorder data as it arrives with NIC hardware Most networks rely on protocol processing or receive-side buffering to handle out-of-order packets, which can add latency and memory overhead. DAQIRI can now offload packet reordering tasks to supported NVIDIA ConnectX-7 or newer NICs, preserving CPU and GPU resources for analysis. For compatible sequence formats, the NIC parses sequence fields and places each payload directly into its ordered position in memory. The application receives the assembled, ordered data without requiring a separate software reorder copy step. Hardware-based reordering is defined here for a specific receive queue. The configuration dictates how to parse the sequence number from the packet header, which reordering method to use, and how missing packets should be handled. - name: "rx_reorder_seq_1024" reorder_engine: "hw" # NIC places payloads in order cyclic_sequence: true # Confirm compatible cyclic numbering missing_action: “drop” # Drop partial batches on RX timeout reorder_type: "gpu" # Deliver packets to GPU memory memory_region: "Reorder_RX_GPU" payload_byte_offset: 42 # Skip 42-byte Ethernet/IPv4/UDP header packet_size: 8192 # Payload bytes per output slot flow_ids: [201] # Apply reorder to RX flow 201 method: seq_packets_per_batch: # Reorder by one sequence field sequence_number: bit_offset: 336 # Sequence starts at bit 336 bit_width: 32 # 32-bit sequence field packets_per_batch: 1024 # 1024 packets per output buffer Use the ibverbs engine for efficient acquisition DAQIRI introduces an ibverbs engine for high-rate receive and transmit of raw Ethernet packets. Built on libibverbs and NVIDIA DevX, the engine is selected by default for raw Ethernet streams. Developers can also select it explicitly by adding engine: “ibverbs” to their DAQIRI configuration, without changing how they use the application API. By reducing per-packet CPU overhead, the ibverbs engine delivers approximately twice the per-core throughput of the previous default DPDK backend at small packet sizes (up to 1024 bytes) and extreme data rates (greater than 200 Gbps), based on benchmark tests performed on the NVIDIA DGX Spark , NVIDIA IGX Thor , and NVIDIA RTX PRO server platforms. Figure 3. The DAQIRI ibverbs engine nearly doubles throughput for 64-byte and 256-byte packets compared with DPDK, while maintaining similar throughput for 8 KB packets. Results shown are from single-queue benchmarks on NVIDIA IGX Thor Reduce feedback latency with direct polling Intelligent instruments may require latency-sensitive feedback from GPU analysis to adjust acquisition or control settings. The DAQIRI direct polling mode reduces communication latency by letting the application thread receive and submit packets directly, eliminating the handoff to a separate I/O worker. In cabled loopback benchmark tests, application send-to-receive latency on the order of 2-4 µs has been demonstrated in direct polling mode. When using the ibverbs engine, developers can select direct polling for control queues while retaining batched processing for high-throughput data streams.

title: Build Tool-Calling Parsers in Rust with AI Agents
abstract:
A tool call can arrive in pieces, an argument can be cut short, or model-specific markup can leak into the answer. A frontend parser turns that output, received as token IDs or decoded text, into visible text, reasoning, and tool calls an application can use. In this post, you’ll learn how tool-call parsing works and use an AI agent to build a parser for a new model. You’ll start with a weather request and a human-reviewed test set, using frontend-crates , the reusable Rust components behind NVIDIA Dynamo tool-calling parsers. Suppose you ask for the weather in Paris. The model may generate reasoning followed by a get_weather call with a city argument. The frontend prepares and tokenizes the prompt, then an inference engine runs the LLM to generate tokens. The parser consumes token IDs or decoded text and separates reasoning, visible text, and tool calls in order. A protocol adapter turns those events into an OpenAI-compatible response, using the same parsing path for batch JSON and streaming updates. Figure 1. The LLM generates tokens; the parser accepts token IDs or decoded text before response shaping The tricky part is recognizing where each piece starts and ends. A call can be malformed or incomplete, a marker can appear inside an argument, or ordinary text can surround the call. The parser has to handle these boundaries without losing data, duplicating calls, or leaking model-specific markup. Returning to the weather request: the model might stop halfway through a city name or call a tool that wasn’t offered. Either can disrupt the agent’s next action. The following NVIDIA Nemotron examples show these two failures. Syntax error. The argument and tool-call frame never close, so no complete call can be parsed. </think><tool_call>
<function=get_weather><parameter=city>Par Semantic error. The frame is valid, but the named tool is absent from the request. </think><tool_call>
<function=unknown_tool><parameter=city>Paris</parameter></function>
</tool_call> These failures require different handling. If the model names an unavailable tool, the parser reports the call it received, and the serving layer validates tool availability, authorization, schema, and call policy. Changing the tool name would hide what the model actually generated. An incomplete call is harder to judge while the stream is open. The rest of the city name may arrive in the next chunk, and a marker can split across chunks, too. Emit too early and syntax leaks into the answer; wait too long and ordinary text gets delayed. The parser needs consistent rules for what to emit, what to buffer, and how to handle the end of the stream. A parser can encounter an unbounded range of inputs. With invalid input, it must follow documented recovery rules rather than guess the model’s intent. Even a syntactically valid call that conforms to the schema can be the wrong choice for the user’s request. The parser needs a consistent grammar and recovery policy so it can preserve valid data without inventing calls or leaking model-specific markup. To check those decisions, frontend-crates pairs model outputs with expected results in a shared Conformance Corpus. Using the Conformance Corpus Use the Conformance Corpus to check how applicable parsers handle behavior first observed in one model. Its language-neutral YAML fixtures pair fixed input with expected output, so Rust parsers and Python references can run the same cases. A regression test for leaked markup, duplicate calls, or lost arguments can cover other families when adapted to their grammars. For a new parser, start with all UNIFIED.* cases across model families. They cover complete, malformed, truncated, multiple, and interleaved calls, plus streaming boundaries and end-of-input behavior. Adapt inputs to your model’s grammar and request settings, add model-specific edge cases, and explain exclusions. You can’t test every possible output, but you can reuse cases from other formats. Table 1 shows the UNIFIED.1-tool_only case from the Parser Conformance Table . In this example, the GOLDEN test set pairs four model-specific inputs with the same expected result: get_weather with city set to Paris. The markers differ, but each case tests the same behavior. Adapting the input format makes the same behavioral test reusable across models. Model Native input Beam <|start|> assistant to=get_weather <|channel|> analysis <|constrain|> xml <|message|> <rfl:parameter name="city"> Paris </rfl:parameter> <|call|> GPT-OSS <|start|> assistant <|channel|> commentary to=functions.get_weather <|constrain|> json <|message|> {"city": "Paris"} <|call|> Muse Spark <|start|> assistant to=get_weather <|message|><atem:function_calls> <atem:invoke name="get_weather"> <atem:parameter name="city"> Paris </atem:parameter> </atem:invoke> </atem:function_calls><|eom|> NVIDIA Nemotron 3 </think> <tool_call> <function= get_weather > <parameter=city> Paris </parameter> </function> </tool_call> Table 1. Model-specific inputs with the same expected GOLDEN output: get_weather({“city”:”Paris”}) Tutorial: Create a new parser Now you can create a parser for a model that frontend-crates doesn’t support yet. Ask your AI agent to read this post and work through the tutorial, starting with the prompt in step 1. Your model’s specification defines the grammar; the shared cases provide behaviors to test. You’ll need a frontend-crates checkout, Rust and Cargo, and the conformance dependencies. The parser exercise runs on a CPU using fixed test fixtures, so you don’t need a GPU. End-to-end testing also requires a working Dynamo runtime, discovery services, and hardware for your model. When you’re ready to test end-to-end, launch the tests with Dynamo runtime on the actual model and GPU(s). The workflow in Figure 2 starts with the model’s grammar, recovery rules, and reviewed GOLDEN expectations. The agent writes or fixes the parser, runs tests, and uses failures to guide the next change. If it proposes changing the expected behavior, review that decision before accepting it. Test your parser end to end with real models before claiming deployment support. Plan time to allocate a machine, load the model, initialize the runtime, and run your own test cases. Turn failures into unit tests for the agent, then rerun the end-to-end test to check the fix. Figure 2. Iterate with unit tests, then test with real models. Turn end-to-end failures into regression tests before continuing 1. Start with a prompt Give the agent this prompt: In the frontend-crates checkout, follow .agents/skills/tool-parser-generator/SKILL.md to create a v2 Unified parser for [MODEL_NAME]. Research its grammar and prepare the GOLDEN test set, adapting applicable UNIFIED.* cases. Pause for human review. After approval, implement, validate, and provide the local conformance report URL for human inspection. 2. Define the GOLDEN test set The GOLDEN test set defines the behavior your parser will be tested against. Use the prompt in step 1 to have the agent generate an initial test set in conformance/fixtures-unified-v2/families/<name>/inputs_and_golden.yaml , independently of parser results. Each case pairs an input with its expected output, called GOLDEN. If those expectations are wrong, the parser can pass the tests and still behave incorrectly. The following example pairs an input with its expected GOLDEN output. It omits request definitions, tools, initialization, and chunk settings; the existing nemotron_v3/inputs_and_golden.yaml shows the full format. family: nemotron_v3
cases: UNIFIED.tool_only.nemotron_v3: input: |- </think><tool_call> <function=get_weather> <parameter=city>Paris</parameter> </function></tool_call> golden: - kind: tool_call name: get_weather arguments: {city: Paris} Ask the agent for an adversarial review, then go through the set manually, case by case. The initial test set may contain errors because expected behavior depends on context the agent may not have.

title: Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments
abstract: When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability. Today we extend that autonomy to AWS Marketplace , so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, and pay in USD on the agent developer’s AWS bill, removing the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys. Figure 1: Overview of AgentCore payments showing the new AWS Billing integration for purchasing on AWS Marketplace Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway . Existing guardrails carry over, developers can set spending limits and approved sellers using AgentCore policy, and the payment session cap is enforced by AgentCore payments, so an agent is unable to overspend. Transactions are auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer . Because agent purchases run through AWS accounts on both sides, agentic purchasing meets the security and auditability enterprises expect. The x402 catalog on AWS Marketplace is expanding with a growing roster of trusted, verified sellers. Tavily, a live search provider for agentic commerce, is one of them: Agentic commerce isn’t just about giving agents the ability to pay. It’s about giving enterprises the confidence to let them. That conviction is driving Tavily’s collaboration with the AWS team on the design of Agentic Commerce. By bringing secure, x402 powered transactions to AWS Marketplace and connecting agents with trusted, KYC verified providers, AWS is laying the foundation for autonomous commerce at production scale. This is what enterprise ready agentic commerce looks like. — Rotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily Today’s launch adds AWS Billing as a payment option in AgentCore payments. An agent can now pay x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers per request, in USD, settling on their AWS bill. When an AWS Marketplace seller responds with 402 Payment Required, its response includes a signed quote for the purchase. With AWS Billing, the agent can forward the seller’s x402 response to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks session budgets, then returns a payment token. The agent retries the request to the seller with the payment token included and receives a successful response. AWS bills the charge to the AWS account where Payment Manager is set up, and the charge appears on that account’s AWS bill. To set up AWS Marketplace purchasing, the developer creates a Payment Manager with an AWS Billing connector. The connector only requires you to set up a service-linked role to access AWS Marketplace. Then, for each task, developers can create a payment session with a spending limit and give the agent the session ID. An agent’s first purchase from a seller creates an agreement for the AWS account with that seller, and AWS Marketplace automatically tracks later purchases against it. Each product will then show up as an AWS Marketplace line item. If your organization uses Private Marketplace , agents can only buy the products it allows. In addition, to discover new sellers, we are launching a new AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway . This optional integration helps agents find products and their endpoints. At launch, AWS Billing supports the x402 exact scheme, where the seller quotes a fixed price for each request. In this post, we walk through a research agent that discovers a tool, pays for a single request through AWS Billing, and answers with sources, with nothing set up in advance. We also provide an accompanying GitHub sample that you can use to evaluate the setup in your own AWS account. Suppose a financial analyst asks the agent what was announced about agentic payments this week. The model wasn’t trained on this week’s news, so the agent looks for a search tool. Through AgentCore Gateway, it searches AWS Marketplace, reads the listing from Tavily, an AWS Marketplace seller, and requests the listing’s x402 endpoints. The agent calls the endpoint and receives an x402 payload with price details. The agent then forwards the x402 payload to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks it against the remaining session budget and returns a payment token. Once these checks are passed, the agent sends the request again with the token attached, and gets the search results. Its answer includes sources and states what it bought and what it cost. In this workflow, agents can apply their reasoning to decide which AWS Marketplace tool to use. Figure 2: End-to-end flow of the sample solution using a Strands agent 1. Discover. The agent calls three read-only gateway tools in order: search listings, get a listing, and list its fulfillment options. Search listings tool only returns endpoints that accept x402. The last call returns the seller’s endpoint URL and the payment protocols it accepts. 2. Get a quote. The agent calls the endpoint with no payment attached. The seller answers with HTTP 402 and puts a signed quote in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header. AWS Marketplace checks the signature against the seller’s registered key, which means a quote with an altered price gets rejected. 3. Pay. The agent passes the quote to the ProcessPayment API with the payment type AWS_BILLING_X402 . If budget remains in the session, AgentCore payments issues a payment token. If not, the call fails and the developer is not charged. 4. Redeem. The agent sends the request again, this time with the token in the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header, and the seller returns the content. Payment tokens are valid for about five minutes, so the agent completes steps 2 through 4 in a single pass. 5. Settle. On the developer’s first purchase from a seller, AWS Marketplace creates the agreement with that seller. After that it meters each charge to their AWS bill. Settlement runs asynchronously and shows up in their AWS bill monthly. To create an AWS Billing connector, developers’ AWS accounts must have the AWS Marketplace service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForMarketplaceAgenticCommerce . AWS Marketplace uses this role to bill AWS Marketplace purchases that their agents make to their AWS account. Refer to the documentation for more details. The open-source GitHub sample in the agentcore-samples repository runs through a demo of the new functionality. It can help you configure AgentCore payments for AWS Marketplace, connect Tavily, run the agent, and inspect the transaction. You can refer to the documentation for more details. setup_aws_billing.py creates a payment manager with an AWS Billing connector, plus the AWS Marketplace service-linked role and three separate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. The session role can set budgets but can’t pay. Meanwhile the agent role can pay but can’t create sessions, so the agent has no way to raise its own budget. setup_gateway.py creates an AgentCore Gateway with the AWS Marketplace connector and gives the agent role the appropriate permissions to use it. The gateway’s role is limited to three read-only AWS Marketplace actions. If you choose to skip this step, you can instead set SELLER_URL in the environment variables to the seller’s endpoint, and the agent will pay that URL only rather than using AgentCore Gateway discovery. The script creates a payment session as the session role and then runs the agent as the agent role. By default the session budget is $0.05 and the per-request cap is $0.02. The agent searches, looks at listings, gets an endpoint, and pays once. In this test run against a $0.01 seller, it compared two listings before buying: When the run finishes, the sample will print the payment with its amount, AWS Marketplace product ID, and processPaymentId . The AWS Marketplace meters charges asynchronously, so the Tavily line item takes a moment to appear on your bill. Agent purchases will also show up in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. Run cleanup.

title: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers
abstract: When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought. At the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This software is augmented by the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system of more than 1,300 microservices providing digital services for 24 million vehicles in the field. In regulated industry, the bar for (software) quality, stability, and governance compliance is exceptionally high. While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge. Scaling agentic AI across a large organization cannot be achieved by isolated teams. It requires collective effort, locally driven experimentation, and active knowledge sharing across the enterprise. This creates a fundamental governance dichotomy: Development teams need the freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without that balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work. This presents a real challenge given hundreds of globally distributed teams building agents across the BMW Group. In this post, we detail the practices and patterns that support BMW’s R&D teams in building, governing and operating agents at scale without sacrificing speed, quality or compliance. Our premise is straightforward: build agents that can cooperate from the start. This requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable, without requiring a single framework or toolchain. Central to this architecture is the agent harness, a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM). It provides the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks for autonomous operation. Just as the AWS Well-Architected Framework standardized cloud infrastructure design, agentic systems need equivalent patterns, reusable blueprints encoding governance, composability, and operational best practices from the start. We organize our solution around five interlocking practices, drawn from hands-on experience building and operating agentic systems at enterprise scale since 2023. Each practice is codified as infrastructure as code (IaC), making adoption repeatable, auditable, and enforceable across teams without blocking DevOps velocity. Governance must be structural from the start and maintained across the full lifecycle. We advocate for three properties of effective agentic governance: Framework-agnostic and externalized: Governance rules such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting and content filtering are enforced at the integration layer. This includes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, a central agent registry and orchestration boundary, rather than within individual agent codebases. This means governance survives framework migrations, model swaps, and team reorganizations. Domain-sensitive and graduated: Not every agent action carries the same risk: drafting documentation, updating customer records, and production database writes demand very different levels of oversight. We implement graduated trust through per-step autonomy levels: Assign trust levels per step, not per agent. A single workflow can include steps at all three levels, so teams can start conservatively and incrementally increase autonomy as confidence builds, grounded in measurable evaluation data, not assumptions. Deterministically enforced: Governance runs as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop. In practice, this happens mainly in the CI/CD pipeline. Permission checks, policy-as-code rules, and compliance validations gate every deployment there, before an agent reaches production. Because these checks run separately from the agent, neither the agent nor its prompts are in a position to override them. Egress controls (recipient allowlisting, outbound secret scanning) help prevent an agent holding confidential data from disclosing it through an otherwise legitimate call. Observability in agentic systems goes beyond traditional application monitoring. The real question is no longer whether a service returned an HTTP 200 status, but whether an agent produced a faithful, policy-compliant output, and how this can be demonstrated through observable execution traces. Answering that requires a ground-truth dataset covering common queries and edge cases. This dataset is used for evaluation from day one, so quality is measured against representative and appropriately governed evaluation datasets for evaluation, not synthetic prompts. This infrastructure cannot be retrofitted and must be part of the initial design. The continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline enforces this, so agents lacking instrumentation fail validation before evaluation runs. We recommend instrumenting three dimensions: For distributed cloud systems, the industry solved the complexity of end-to-end workflows by adopting architectural patterns such as microservices or service meshes. The evolution of agentic systems needs to follow a similar trajectory, moving from monolithic, generalist agents toward multiple collaborating specialized agents. Teams should define the problem before considering agents’ functionality. Before writing any orchestration logic, they should produce five concrete artifacts: This discipline prevents the most common failure modes we observe: agents that take on too many responsibilities accumulate bloated prompts, reducing accuracy and increasing latency. Once a single agent is well-scoped, it must be designed as a composable building block. Therefore, we define a three-tier composition hierarchy: Each tier is validated independently in the CI/CD pipeline. Component tests cover tools and skills, interaction tests cover their composition into flows. These tiers are connected through open standards: MCP and Agent Skills for tool integration, the protocol for agent-to-agent communication, and OpenTelemetry for observability across the resulting interactions. Figure 1 shows how the three tiers build on each other, from individual MCP tools at the base to complete flows at the top. Figure 1: Three-tier system to build composable agents In production, even well-scoped agents can break down as real-world usage diverges from what was anticipated at design time: query patterns shift, tool-selection logic struggles, and performance degrades unpredictably. The right response is to decompose complex agents into multiple specialized ones, each with clearer instructions, simpler tool sets, and more focused reasoning. The benefits are concrete: Complexity can be reduced along two axes: Critically, since each specialized agent only accesses the data and tools required for its role, this architecture helps to enforce least-privilege by design, a compliance requirement in regulated industries. Realizing these benefits, however, requires that agents can find and interoperate with each other. To prevent the emergence of AI islands , we maintain a centralized registry of agents, tools, and skills. This registry serves as: The shift from managing individual agents to governing an agent fleet requires agent architectures to be codified. Using Infrastructure-as-code frameworks such as Terraform or AWS CloudFormation , teams provision and manage agent infrastructure with the same rigor applied to any production system: All three are enforced as pipeline gates, validated before registration, not audited after the fact. The adoption model is deliberately bottom-up with central curation. Individual teams build skills and MCP tools to solve their immediate problems. All teams can contribute by sharing their assets through the registry.

title: Run your whole selling business in AWS Quick
abstract: Most sellers do not need another AI product to learn. They need the tools and information they already use brought together, so they can see what is happening in their business and act on it. AWS Quick and the Amazon Selling Partner plugin do that together. Quick brings an Amazon seller’s sales data, inventory signals, and marketplace intelligence into one place, where questions become answers and answers become actions. It understands the seller’s full business context, so the seller does not need to re-explain their catalog, their margins, or their competitive landscape in every conversation. It is built on AWS, the same infrastructure Amazon uses to run its own marketplace. At Amazon Accelerate on September 23, 2026, Amazon announced the Selling Partner plugin and launched it in beta in AWS Quick. This post covers what launched, how to claim the free AWS Quick offer, and what the experience looks like day to day. It also covers how the skills and connectors work when a seller puts them to use. Limited-time offer: 12 months of AWS Quick Plus, free. Every primary selling account holder worldwide can claim a free 12-month subscription, plus access for 10 additional users you delegate. Sign up by December 31, 2026. Claim your free AWS Quick Plus offer. Four things make Quick a fit for how Amazon sellers already work: it learns the business, it reaches beyond the Amazon store, it turns data into decisions, and it protects seller data on infrastructure sellers already trust. Quick and the Selling Partner plugin connect to a seller’s inventory feeds, sales data, and operational documents. From these, Quick builds a living understanding of the catalog structure, margin thresholds, seasonality, and competitive position. Ask Quick to audit your ASINs for Q4, and it returns a ranked recommendation built on the seller’s real margin data, historical conversion, and inventory availability. Its recommendations get sharper the more the seller works with it. A seller’s business runs across many tools: a storefront on another channel, an email inbox, an accounting system, spreadsheets, a supplier portal. Quick connects to where the seller already works and pulls context from across the whole operation. It is a business assistant that happens to know Amazon deeply, so the seller grows overall, not on one channel alone. Sellers are not short on data. They have Brand Analytics, Search Query Performance, advertising reports, inventory health, and listing quality data. The problem is turning those signals into one clear action. Quick does the synthesis. It watches for change, flags what matters, builds the analysis, and presents the decision with the evidence behind it. Quick runs on AWS and does not use seller data to train models, not for general improvement and not for anything else. Seller data stays in the seller’s environment and never informs anyone else’s models. For a seller already operating on the Amazon marketplace, there is no new security posture to evaluate.
