The infrastructure is the same one protecting the seller account today, and the seller’s chosen AWS Region governs where data stays. The Selling Partner plugin connects AWS Quick directly to live Seller Central data. After one sign-in with a Seller Central account, the plugin gives conversational access to product listings, inventory, and sales data, pulled live rather than exported and reassembled by hand. It installs like an app, with no coding required. It ships with curated Amazon skills, and it pairs with Amazon Ads MCP so campaign performance and spend sit next to the selling data. The plugin is in beta for US stores. Figure 1: The Selling Partner plugin consent screen, where the seller grants None, View, or Edit access per data category The permission screen is worth a pause. The seller grants access per data category, choosing None, View, or Edit for each, and reviews an agreement before authorizing. Nothing is all-or-nothing, and access can be narrowed or revoked later. Figure 2: Connecting the Selling Partner plugin from the AWS Quick sign-up flow After the plugin is connected, the work happens in a conversation. You ask in plain language, Quick pulls the relevant live data, and it comes back with an answer and a recommended next step. Instead of checking a dashboard, exporting a report, and reconciling it in a spreadsheet, you move from a question to an answer to an action in one place. You review what Quick proposes before anything is sent. Figure 3: Quick diagnosing whether a sales dip comes from traffic or conversion, using live selling data At the Accelerate workshop we had sellers build real agents live, from a plain-language description, in a few minutes. Quick turns the description into a working agent, which the seller then refines in conversation. The seller is staging a new product into Amazon and wants the lowest total landed cost. The agent reads supplier data and weighs the fulfillment options per SKU on inbound cost, storage, and speed to sellable. It walks through placement choices and returns the output the seller picks: a shipping plan, a cost comparison, or a combined packet. It explains its reasoning and confirms before it creates anything. Figure 4: The Inventory Launch Prep agent comparing FBA and AWD fulfillment per factor and recommending a hybrid approach After the launch, the agent reads four signal families through the Selling Partner plugin: listing health, inventory, sales, and traffic. It connects them to find the cause rather than just reporting numbers. Flat sales with healthy traffic points to a conversion problem. Flat sales with falling traffic points to discoverability. Good conversion with falling units points to supply. It returns a health summary per ASIN, the diagnosis with evidence, and a ranked fix list, labeling any low-confidence call. Figure 5: The Post-Launch Product Health agent’s weekly summary, with week-over-week sales evidence One honest limit, handled honestly: the selling data does not include cost of goods, so the agent reports margin after Amazon fees and labels it that way. When the seller wants true gross margin, the agent asks them to bring their cost numbers into the conversation. It never presents after-fees margin as if it were gross margin. The Selling Partner plugin and Amazon Ads MCP bring the Amazon selling and advertising data into Quick. Other connectors in AWS Quick bring in the rest of how the business runs, organized by role. These include a second storefront (orders and products from another channel), email and calendar (draft a supplier note, track what is due), team messaging (share an update), and accounting and inventory systems (cost and stock context the selling data does not carry). Because the pieces sit together, the seller can ask one question that reaches across Amazon data and the tools around it. At Accelerate, Richard Brown, who runs the sneaker care brand Proof Culture and sells across five stores including Amazon, showed what this looks like. He had built his own AI assistant over time, and the hard part was never the AI. It was getting his selling data connected in real time. “The hard part was never the AI. The hard part was getting my selling data into it, and that is the part that is now simple with the plugin. With Quick and the Selling Partner plugin, just connect your account and start asking questions.” — Richard Brown, Proof Culture, at Amazon Accelerate 2026 In his demo, Richard asked Quick about upcoming sneaker drops and checked whether he had enough FBA stock to cover a major release. He had Quick model how far his current inventory would carry him. Then he asked it to draft a reorder purchase order and a message to his team. A morning of research across different tools took a few minutes. Claim your free year of AWS Quick Plus Read the AWS Quick documentation Media captured from the Amazon Accelerate 2026 workshop ‘Build It Live: Automate New Product Launch in AWS Quick.

title: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints
abstract: Every inference endpoint is well tuned the day it goes into production. Teams choose an instance type, serving configuration, and scaling settings that suit the model and its traffic at launch. With the endpoint serving smoothly, they understandably move on to the next priority. The workload, however, rarely stays still. Traffic patterns evolve, prompts grow longer, serving engines such as vLLM ship new releases, SageMaker inference develops new optimization techniques, and new fine-tuned checkpoints change the resources your model needs. Over time, a well-tuned endpoint quietly drifts. Latency and time to first token edge upward. A configuration that was never quite ideal keeps missing available performance gains. A GPU provisioned for demand that never materialized sits idle week after week. Because nothing has failed, no alarm sounds, and the drift goes unnoticed until users feel it or the bill reflects it. Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost by using Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature with Agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio . Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints using vLLM serving containers and GPU instances, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. From those signals, it surfaces three kinds of findings: SageMaker AI sends a finding through AWS Health, with one notification per endpoint that covers that endpoint’s findings. When a notification arrives, you can act on it in one place. It opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio with the endpoint, and its recent traffic already filled in. From there, you run inference recommendations to benchmark your current configuration against alternatives and compare them side by side on response time, throughput, and cost per million tokens. That turns a judgment call into a decision backed by data. Benchmarks run on separate compute, and nothing changes on your endpoint until you choose to apply a result. In this post, we show how SageMaker AI monitors your endpoints and how to read the notifications it sends through AWS Health. We then show how to go from a notification to a benchmarked decision in SageMaker Studio. We walk through three example scenarios, show how to apply or dismiss a recommendation safely, and explain how to opt an endpoint out of monitoring. SageMaker AI inference recommendations follow a four-step loop: observe, notify, recommend, and decide. Each step is designed so that you stay in control, and your production endpoint isn’t changed without your explicit action. The feature produces a few types of findings. The following table summarizes what triggers each one and what gets tested when you choose to benchmark. Monitoring itself needs no setup, it is on by default. The following prerequisites apply when you choose to act on a finding by running a benchmark and, optionally, applying a change: Cost note: Monitoring has no GPU cost. Benchmarks use standard SageMaker AI charges, or your machine learning (ML) reservation if you have one. You receive notifications in AWS Health on the console and by email and each one follows the same structure, so it’s quick to scan: Notifications report observations and label estimates. No benchmark has run at this point. A representative notification reads as follows: Subject: [Action may be required] SageMaker AI inference improvements for your endpoint SageMaker AI tracks the latency and capacity usage of your inference endpoints by default, and found improvements for one of them. It does not read your requests or responses. What we noticed: Over the past week, time to first token on this endpoint increased compared with the week before. Recommended action: Open SageMaker Studio to benchmark alternatives on separate compute. Your production endpoint is not changed. Cadence : Each endpoint gets one notification that covers the applicable findings. You get at most one notification per endpoint at a time, covering all its findings, and SageMaker AI limits how many an account receives at once. Notifications are AWS Region specific, so you see an endpoint’s findings when you’re signed in to that endpoint’s Region. In this section, we review a few scenarios of endpoint optimizations that will trigger findings to be reported. A team runs a chat assistant on a single SageMaker AI endpoint. They add retrieval to improve answer quality, so every request now carries pages of retrieved context and prompts get much longer. Nothing breaks, and no alarm they set trips, but responses start more slowly. SageMaker AI compares the endpoint’s median (p50) time to first token and median end-to-end latency with the previous week. When either one rises enough over the week, it flags the change. Because the comparison is against the endpoint’s own history, the team doesn’t need to set a threshold in advance. The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for a latency drift finding. The message reports that median time to first token rose about 200 ms week over week, and the Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations. Figure 1: AWS Health event for a latency drift finding, with a link to run inference recommendations in SageMaker AI A platform team hosts an internal code-completion model on a SageMaker AI endpoint. They deployed it with default serving settings and never revisited them. The model and serving container support speculative decoding, a technique for faster responses, but it isn’t enabled. SageMaker AI flags this as an opportunity. Whether it helps depends on the endpoint’s traffic, such as how many requests run concurrently and how long prompts and responses are. The notification recommends running inference recommendations, which benchmarks speculative decoding against the endpoint’s recent traffic and shows whether it’s worth turning on. The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for a speculative decoding finding. The message reports that the model and serving container support speculative decoding, but the endpoint doesn’t use it. The Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations. Figure 2: AWS Health event for a speculative decoding finding, with a link to run inference recommendations in SageMaker AI The notification explains that speculative decoding can make responses faster, and that the benchmark compares response time with and without it on the endpoint’s recent traffic. A summarization endpoint was sized for a launch that drew a fraction of the planned audience, so its GPUs sit mostly idle for a week. This scenario also shows a case where the right decision may be to make no change at all. The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for an unused capacity finding. The message reports that for most of the week, even the endpoint’s busiest GPU used 12 percent or less of its capacity. The Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations. Figure 3: AWS Health event for an unused capacity finding, with a link to run inference recommendations in SageMaker AI You can choose Open in SageMaker AI from the recommended actions as shown in the screenshot above to apply or dismiss a recommendation. Lets walk through this in next section. You stay in control throughout, and nothing deploys automatically. When you choose Open in SageMaker AI from a notification’s recommended actions, Amazon SageMaker Studio opens a JupyterLab space and shows the prompt that will run in the agentic chat.

title: Inside Amazon Connect Talent: The science of structured AI interviews
abstract: For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions? Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge. They use consistent, job-related questions and clear scoring criteria to give candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their skills. Decades of research in industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology have shown that structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998; Sackett et al., 2022). Yet delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create q uestions, train interviewers, and evaluate responses consistently . Amazon Connect Talent brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups, and evidence-based scoring to help organizations gather consistent, job-related information while giving more candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their strengths. We built Connect Talent around three core design principles and evaluated how well the service applies them through a combination of internal research and independent expert review. The findings offer a closer look at the science behind Connect Talent’s AI-le d, structured interviewing. Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role. The service uses job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. Each scorecard defines specific strength and concern signals, and every interview question targets the behaviors it aims to uncover. The AI interviewer also adapts to each response. After every answer, it checks whether the candidate has provided enough evidence for the competency being assessed. When details are missing, it asks targeted follow-up questions. This approach preserves the structure of the interview while giving candidates more opportunities to explain their experience. Connect Talent separates the interview conversation from the evaluation. The AI interviewer gathers evidence but does not assign scores. Afterward, a separate evaluation process identifies which behaviors the candidate demonstrated and cites the supporting transcript passa ges. The service calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score. Hiring teams can review the evidence behind each rating, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate. Connect Talent evaluates transcribed candidate responses without using video, voice tone, or physical appearance to calculate competency scores. The service also excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately. These safeguards help focus assessments on job-related behaviors and limit the influence of unrelated information. To understand how well the se design principles work in practice, we combined independent I-O psychology evaluations with internal research. We examined whether the service generates job-relevant interview content, identifies behavioral evidence in line with expert assessments, gathers more complete responses through follow-up questions, and distinguishes between levels of demonstrated competency. The quality of a structured interview starts with the skills it measures. Candidates need questions that reflect the requirements of the role, and hiring teams need confidence that the interview assesses those skills. Amazon engaged an independent I-O psychology firm to evaluate Connect Talent’s AI-generated interview content. The firm reviewed the service’s baseline output before human editing and examined how well its competencies, questions , and rubrics aligned with job requirements. The evaluation found that Connect Talent retained critical job information in 100% of the job descriptions reviewed. Of the competencies generated, 91% were clearly traceable to the job description. The firm’s psychologists also found that 98% of interview questions targeted the intended competencies, and 94% of rubric signals clearly measured the intended competency. These findings show that Connect Talent generated job-relevant interview content that met independent expert criteria in a vast majority of cases. Hiring teams can then review, select, and edit the competencies, scorecards, and questions before using them. This human oversight gives organizations control over the interview process while helping them apply structured hiring practices at scale . Relevant questions provide the foundation for a structured interview. The next challenge is evaluating the evidence candidates provide with consistency. To examine this, an independent I-O psychology firm reviewed 36 interviews assessing whether candidates demonstrated specific strengths and concerns, creating 252 rubric signals. Connect Talent evaluated the same transcripts , reviewed hundreds of rubric signals , and aligned with expert scoring decisions in 89.3% of c ases . Scoring alignment reached 97.6% when candidates provided clear evidence and 92.9% when only considering candidate concern signals, which identify behaviors that may indicate a poor fit for the intended role . The evaluation also produced a Cohen’s kappa of 0.79, a statistical measure that eliminates random chance coincidence . A Cohen’s kappa of 0.79 is just under the standard of 0 .8 1 for almost perfect agreement . This ou tc ome indicates substantial agreement between Connect Talent and the independent expert candidate scoring. Candidates may have relevant experience but leave important details out of their first response. In a traditional one-way video interview, a candidate may receive a fixed question and have only one opportunity to answer it. Hiring teams must then evaluate the information available, even when the response leaves many important questions unanswered. Connect Talent uses adaptive follow-ups to gather more complete evidence. For example, a candidate might describe improving a slow system. The AI interviewer can ask what changed, which actions the candidate took, and how they measured the improvement. These questions help candidates explain their contributions and results in greater detail. We studied the impact of follow-up questions by comparing assessments based on a candidate’s first response with assessments based on the full interview conversation. In a preliminary evaluation, scores based only on the first response were up to 1.14 points lower on a five-point scale than scores based on the full conversation. Assessments using the full conversation also came closer to expert evaluations. Without follow-up questions, the scoring process identified fewer strength signals and more concern signals. In some cases, the candidate’s initial response simply lacked the information needed to demonstrate a relevant behavior. The full conversation captured more of what candidates demonstrated and gave hiring teams a more complete record of their experience. Hiring teams need scores that reflect meaningful differences in demonstrated skills. Yet research has found that some AI scoring approaches concentrate ratings within a narrow range, making those differences harder to recognize (Zhu et al., 2026). Connect Talent uses behaviorally anchored scorecards to evaluate specific strength and concern signals. Rather than asking an AI model to assign an overall rating, the service identifies evidence for each behavior and calculates the competency score using a predefined formula. Consider the competency “collaboration”. A general AI scoring approach might evaluate a candidate’s overall collaboration skills based on the interview transcript.

title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
abstract: When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund. We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop. With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints. There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use. Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself. You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability. AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment. Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults: Customer-provided Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Browser, Code Interpreter, inline functions, skills, memory, and customer-provided containers continue to work through the existing harness interfaces. Harness manages its defaults so that agents using them receive the current AgentCore recommended experience as models, instructions, context management, and built-in capabilities improve. Explicit configuration always takes precedence: When allowedTools is omitted or set to ["*"] , Harness provides the current recommended built-in tool set. Because this set can gain capabilities over time, applications with a fixed security or capability boundary should list only the tools they need. For example, the following configuration permits read-only filesystem access and web retrieval without granting shell access or file modification: With lifecycle hooks, you can run your own deterministic code at defined points in the agent loop. For example, an AWS Lambda function can allow or deny a request or a tool call, and an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic or Amazon EventBridge event bus can receive a notification to record activity or start an asynchronous workflow. Harness supports four lifecycle events: Only Lambda hooks can change the agent loop. They run synchronously and return allow or deny, with an optional reason. SNS and Amazon EventBridge hooks are notifications and don’t block the agent loop. For example, a customer-support agent can investigate an order on its own while a before_tool_call hook checks each refund against an approval limit before the refund tool runs. The following configuration attaches that Lambda function to the harness: The function receives the proposed tool call in the hook payload and returns a decision: When the function denies the call, the harness skips the refund and the agent continues, so it can tell the customer that the request was escalated. Each decision also appears in the InvokeHarness response stream as a hookEvent : Hooks also apply to subagents. When the agent delegates a task, each tool call the subagent makes runs through the same beforeToolCall and afterToolCall hooks, so delegation can’t bypass your refund policy. The invocation-level hooks ( beforeInvocation , afterInvocation ) run once for the whole invocation. You configure hooks with CreateHarness or UpdateHarness . If a Lambda function times out or returns an error, the hook applies its failureMode , which defaults to deny. For timeouts, payload fields, and context limits, see Lifecycle hooks in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide . To see every event and target type working together, try the Refund Desk sample in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub . A six-step guided tour shows all four lifecycle events and the AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge targets. It also shows validation of client-supplied inline function results and the difference between failureMode deny and allow. Creating a harness takes a single command. You name it and set up the instructions, context policy, and limits you want. This example creates a Research Coordinator: a harness with a task-oriented system prompt and summarization-based truncation. In a single invocation, it runs a researcher, a synthesizer, and a reviewer as subagents and returns one consolidated report. You get multi-agent orchestration and context management without provisioning infrastructure or wiring the delegation yourself. The agentcore harness commands call the harness APIs directly, so you don’t need a CLI project or a deployment step. Install the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with npm: The CLI uses your default AWS credentials. It has no --profile flag, so set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable if you want a specific profile. Save the coordinator’s instructions from the sample as system_prompt.md in your working directory. This command passes the coordinator’s system prompt, a summarization policy that keeps the 30 most recent messages intact as the conversation grows, and limits high enough for the full workflow. Because it omits the model, memory, and execution role, the harness uses the current AgentCore recommended model and managed memory, and the CLI creates an execution role in IAM for you. Creation is asynchronous. Wait for creation to finish. The last command should print READY : Invoke your harness with a new session ID. Start with a basic question. The coordinator answers it directly, without calling its subagents: Then ask for a full research report in the same session. The coordinator plans the work and delegates to the researcher, synthesizer, and reviewer in order. It runs at most one revision cycle if the reviewer asks for it, and delivers the final report. Reusing the session ID continues the conversation in the same environment. With --prompt , the CLI prints the completed transcript as JSON when the turn finishes. The research run takes about 10 to 15 minutes. To follow along as it works, leave out --prompt , and the CLI opens an interactive chat. The same example in Python (boto3), including the full system prompt, is available in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. Delete the harness when you’re done. This also deletes its managed memory unless you pass --delete-managed-memory false .

title: Amazon Polly launches voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand
abstract: Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of audio recordings from a speaker who has agreed to have their voice cloned, and Amazon Polly builds your own cloned voice in that speaker’s voice. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning launches with seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region. Access is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. Others can reach out to their AWS account team or apply for access to get access. With this new feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications. Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis, see Amazon Polly Pricing page for details. Press play: the first few seconds are a real recording of the speaker, and then their cloned voice takes over with words they never recorded. A consistent brand voice across channels Establish one recognizable voice and use it across your interactive voice response (IVR) system, cascaded voice agents, mobile app, in-store announcements, advertising, and connected devices. Rather than relying on a generic stock voice or re-booking a recording session each time a script changes, you can generate on-brand audio on demand, with a consistent sound in every channel. Deliver a distinctive, on-brand voice across self-service flows, and update prompts as offers and policies change without a new studio session. You can create prompts from source text, test them before rollout, and use the same voice across greeting, routing, and notification experiences. Creators, publishers, and studios can create audiobooks, courses, podcasts, game characters, and videos in multiple custom voices to enhance the listening experience, and produce subsequent chapters or updates quickly. Localization with a consistent persona Maintain a recognizable voice identity across a content library, so narration remains coherent across titles and updates. Each cloned voice speaks only the language it was recorded in. For multilingual experiences, create and review approved voices per supported language. Accessibility and personalization Offer a natural, human-sounding voice for reading experiences, assistive tools, and personalized interactions. You confirm the speaker’s consent each time you create a voice. With voice cloning, you can build a custom Amazon Polly voice from recordings of a single speaker and then synthesize speech in that voice through the Amazon Polly generative engine. The voice moves through four steps, from recording the speaker to using the finished voice: Figure 1: The voice cloning lifecycle, from recording a speaker to using the finished voice A cloned voice goes through four steps: A cloned voice is made from one person’s recordings. You confirm that you have the speaker’s consent for all recordings and that you control who can use the voice and when it’s deleted. For details on intended uses and limitations, see the Amazon Polly AI Service Card and the AWS Responsible Use of AI guidance. Your cloned voice learns from the recording, including the parts you’d rather it didn’t: the laptop fan, the room echo, the meeting app’s noise filter. On the console: once voice cloning is enabled for your account (see Availability), expand the left panel and choose Voice cloning , upload up to 10 recordings or select them from Amazon S3, confirm the terms, and choose Create . Each upload can be up to 5 MB. When the voice is ready, try it out on its details page. If Python reports that the Polly object has no attribute create_voice , upgrade boto3. For long texts such as audiobook chapters or course modules, use an asynchronous synthesis task that writes the audio to S3: For additional end-to-end Speech AI applications you can build with Amazon Polly, including the voice cloning feature, such as cascaded voice agents and live speech translators, go to the Amazon Polly GitHub repo . Voice creation takes minutes, so treat it as a provisioning step, not part of a user request. A small workflow (for example, AWS Step Functions or a job queue) can call CreateVoice , check GetVoice every 30 seconds until the voice is active, and then store the voice ID in your configuration. CreateVoice and DeleteVoice share a limit of 1 request per second, so queue bulk creations and deletions. DescribeVoices lists your cloned voices alongside the voices built into Amazon Polly. Cloned voices have Origin set to customer . Store the voice ID, Region, language, consent reference, and owner for each voice, and give each voice a unique Name . If a CreateVoice call times out or returns a server error, the voice might already exist, and the SDK’s automatic retries can create a second one. Check DescribeVoices for that name before you try again. CreateVoice returns ThrottlingException when you exceed the 1-request-per-second limit it shares with DeleteVoice , and ServiceQuotaExceededException when the account has reached its cloned-voice quota in that Region. Synthesizing with, or deleting, a voice that is still being created returns ConflictException . If a voice uses your own KMS key, callers without access to the key get an access-denied error. When creation fails, StatusReason gives only a general message, so check the recordings against the preceding recording best practices, then delete the failed voice and create a new one. Cloned voices are IAM resources, so you can give the role that serves traffic permission to synthesize with one voice of choice. If the voice uses your own KMS key, that role also needs access to the key. Keep polly:CreateVoice and polly:DeleteVoice for a separate provisioning role. Here’s an example policy for the serving role: With tags, you can write the same rule once for a whole group of voices using aws:ResourceTag conditions. Review your existing policies too: a statement that allows polly:SynthesizeSpeech on all resources ( "Resource": "*" ) also covers every cloned voice in the account. Each account has an initial quota of 10 cloned voices per Region. To request an increase, contact your account team or AWS Support . A voice exists only in the account and Region where you created it. To serve another Region or account, create the voice again in that Region from the same recordings, and make sure the speaker’s consent covers every copy. Before a voice goes live, listen to it reading your own content: product names, numbers, addresses, and the longest sentences you have. The same text can come out slightly differently from one request to the next. For fixed prompts such as phone-line greetings, generate the audio once, approve it with the speaker and your brand team, and serve the stored file. If a name or term comes out wrong, spell it differently in the text or use a Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) <phoneme> tag. Phoneme tags work with cloned voices in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish. See Supported SSML tags . Voice cloning in Amazon Polly gives your application a voice people recognize: recorded once, with the speaker’s consent, and ready to use through the Amazon Polly APIs. To get started on the console, make sure Voice cloning is enabled for your account, prepare a recording and the required consent, open the Amazon Polly console , and create your first cloned voice. If you are a new customer and would like to enable voice cloning, reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to get access.

title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
abstract: As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock , token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline. In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality. Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles , one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console , you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce. Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports , handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call. Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste. The goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact. With Amazon Bedrock prompt caching , the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching ). Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing ). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response. Both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires new infrastructure or architecture changes. Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy ( see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing ). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer. Two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains. Semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a new request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings ( see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks ). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that users don’t receive outdated answers. Model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever. The first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching.

title: From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League
abstract: Cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again. AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale. Cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas. In this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI , and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League. AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps: Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges: Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency. Figure 1: AWS AI League champion at AWS re:Invent 2025 Figure 2: 2026 AWS AI League winner at Cisco campus The AWS AI League story at Cisco grows out of a deep engineering partnership. Cisco and AWS bring together networking, cloud, security, and observability for shared customers including: The two companies have also published joint deployment guides and Cisco Validated Designs across networking and AWS. A recent example of co-innovation is SD-WAN fabric on demand across the AWS backbone, built to deliver the resilience and uptime customers expect. “When you see that many business units independently choosing to build their next-generation platforms natively on AWS, that’s not a vendor relationship anymore. It’s a true engineering partnership.” — Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco Cisco’s VP of Engineering Kumaril Kapoor and AWS Industries India leader Chandra Balani sit down to discuss the AWS and Cisco partnership story, from co-innovation across networking, cloud, and AI to enabling thousands of engineers through the annual Cisco AWS Transformation Fest. As the partnership grew, it extended beyond technology to people. Working closely with Cisco teams in India, AWS saw a strong appetite for learning and experimenting among Cisco engineers across many business units. The question was how to scale that impact beyond the day-to-day touchpoints of the partnership. The answer was Cisco Transformation Fest, first held in 2022. The program is built on five tenets the team summarized as SCALE : Figure 3: 2026 Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 4.0 AWS AI League finalists Transformation Fest brings together several formats: AWS GameDays, AWS AI League, sessions where Cisco leaders share best practices and success stories with peers, and sessions on Amazon and AWS culture. What began as a single event is now an annual, three-day program that has completed its fourth edition and reached around 2,000 engineers. AWS continues to engage Cisco teams with hands-on workshops and experience-based accelerations. “It has been genuinely valuable for us, and it’s really a journey, but I appreciate most is the intent behind it. It’s built around our people. It gives our engineers the time, the space, and the hands-on support to grow real skills on AWS. For us, it has turned into a lasting culture of learning by doing. It’s not a one-off event.” — Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco Of all the Transformation Fest formats, AWS AI League has had the most visible impact. Its gamified, hands-on structure puts engineers to work with Amazon SageMaker on fine-tuning, model customization and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for agent building, against a clock and in front of their peers. Participants leave with practical experience and genuine confidence in their AI skills. “This is where enablement actually turns into real execution.” — Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco Hemanth V, a software engineer in Cisco’s switching core platform team, had an inspiring journey that set the benchmark for Cisco. Hemanth finished ahead of Ross Williams from Aqfer (second place) and Deepesh Khanna from Capital One (third place). “You don’t need to know everything beforehand. You will learn a lot of things on the way. The only thing that matters is your curiosity and willingness to learn.” — Hemanth V, Software Engineer, Cisco, and 2025 AWS AI League Champion In 2026, Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0 hosted a full AWS AI League agentic AI tournament. The AWS account team ran pre-event training so that engineers with no prior agentic AI experience could compete from day one. The format was designed to narrow a large field down to a single winner: Nishanth Aluhonnu, a software engineer at Cisco, finished first at every stage and earned a full conference pass to AWS re:Invent 2026. The finale itself showed why the format works. Participants could not change code, tools, or prompts during the finale, only a short steering instruction before each round. Success depended on how well each agent made decisions on maps it had never seen before. Nishanth lost the first round, then won the second by a wide margin by ignoring a board full of low-value coins in favor of a single high-value challenge. Figure 4: Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 4.0 AWS AI League finalists on stage The 2026 winning agent offers lessons that go well beyond the game. Each design choice maps to a decision teams face when they run agents in production. The agentic AI challenge scores agents on challenge points, a treasure bonus, remaining lives, and a token bonus, computed as tokenBonus = 1000 - (totalOutputTokens / challengesVisited) . In the qualifier, the top four agents all solved the map. The first-place agent emitted 1,220 output tokens and the second-place agent emitted 1,430, and the final margin was only 16 points out of nearly 16,000. After every agent can solve the problem, efficiency decides the winner. To understand which tokens mattered, Nishanth built nine variants of the same agent, changing one thing at a time. The result was clear: tool results and the system prompt didn’t count against the score, but everything the agent wrote, including tool call arguments, did. Each tool call carried roughly 52 tokens of fixed overhead on top of its arguments. This mirrors real-world cost. Generating output is sequential and is typically priced several times higher than input, and in an agent loop that cost compounds across every step. A long, well-structured system prompt (which you can also cache) is cheap. A chatty agent isn’t. A common architecture for this challenge is a supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that delegates to specialist sub-agents for navigation, computation, and web retrieval. It’s a sound pattern for many production systems. The winning design used a single agent with no sub-agents. Instead, the prompt began with a short dispatch table that matched each challenge type to the right approach in a single turn. The reasoning was simple: every handoff between agents is a message the model has to write, and in this challenge every written token is scored.

title: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself. Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a new resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery. In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI . A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it. Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas: A few terms describe the pieces: The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. The router doesn’t create capacity, scale your endpoints, deploy models, or copy model artifacts and container images. Each destination must already be running in its Region. Figure 1: Each request goes to a healthy destination, with the router preferring destinations in its own Region The router considers only destinations that are registered on the routing target and that it’s authorized to invoke. Among those, it prefers destinations in its own Region, and when more than one local destination is healthy, it spreads requests across them evenly. Requests leave the Region only when local destinations can’t serve reliably. To detect that, SageMaker AI calculates a health score for each destination from its recent requests, measured in the destination’s own Region. Server errors (5xx), throttles, and timeouts lower the score. Errors from the SageMaker AI platform (for example, failed health check) lower it the most. Errors caused by the request itself, such as invalid input, don’t lower it, because the same request would fail in any Region. Model latency isn’t an input, so an endpoint that keeps returning successful responses keeps its traffic. Signals such as failed instance launches or an endpoint running fewer instances than its autoscaling target make the router react faster, but only after the destination starts failing requests. The router evaluates each destination’s health and publishes it to Amazon CloudWatch as one of three states. A healthy destination serves normally. An overloaded destination still serves, and the router moves part of its traffic away. A degraded destination is failing or can’t serve, so the router moves most of its traffic away and keeps a small share to detect recovery. Figure 2: How each destination health state changes the traffic the router sends to it SageMaker AI manages failover thresholds and timing, so you don’t need to tune any thresholds. If health information for remote destinations goes stale, the router keeps traffic in its own Region, so a gap in monitoring never moves traffic on its own. The more requests fail, the more traffic moves, so a destination need not fail outright first. Traffic starts to move within about a minute of sustained errors, or longer for a destination with little traffic. Traffic that leaves the local Region is spread across the healthy remote destinations in proportion to their health. You can’t set weights or a fallback order. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left. Requests in progress aren’t interrupted. When a destination fails a real-time request without running the model, the router retries that request once on a different destination. This covers, for example, a throttle, a 503 error, a model that isn’t ready, a rejection by a cross-Region traffic cap, or access denied by the destination. The router never retries timeouts, 500 errors, or model errors. For asynchronous requests, the router tries each eligible destination once, local destinations first, until one accepts the request. Figure 3: The router retries a real-time request once on another destination, and only when the model didn’t run Figure 4 shows where requests were served in one of our tests with a test model. Figure 4: Where requests were served as the local endpoint was overloaded, a destination in another account lost and regained access, and the local endpoint recovered The following use cases show common ways to use cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. When a destination belongs to a different account than the router, both accounts must allow each request. On the endpoint side, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, and the sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition key limits that access to one named router. The following policy allows only my-router in account 444455556666 to invoke the endpoint. Its second statement has no router condition and lets the router account read the endpoint’s status. Without that statement, the destination shows its status as unknown. In the router account, callers need sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouter (or sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouterAsync ) on the router and sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint (or sagemaker:InvokeEndpointAsync ) on every destination, because the router invokes each destination on the caller’s behalf. A router never gives a caller access to an endpoint they couldn’t call directly. For DescribeInferenceRouter to report each destination’s status, callers also need sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint on endpoints and sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent on inference components. Applications in other accounts call the router by assuming a role in the router account. For a walkthrough, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI and User Guide on cross-account destinations . Figure 5: Controls the endpoint owner keeps: an endpoint policy that allows one named router, and an optional cross-Region traffic cap When the router moves requests away from a Region that’s short on capacity, those requests land on endpoints that already serve their own Region’s callers. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so a surge of overflow can push it into throttling. With a cross-Region traffic cap, the endpoint owner decides how much of the endpoint’s capacity other Regions might use. You set the cap in CreateEndpointConfig with CrossRegionTrafficConfig , which takes two required values. MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance is the number of invocations per second that one instance can take, which you measure with a load test of your model, instance type, and typical payload.

title: Protect agent tool calls with Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
abstract: In this post, we show how Skyflow and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway keep sensitive data out of the tools your AI agents call, and out of the model context those tools feed. We add Skyflow Detect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway as a request and response interceptor . The Skyflow interceptor de-identifies data before it reaches a tool, restores it before the agent reads the result, and replaces documents with clean copies before the agent opens them. Your agents and tools don’t change. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace, and the interceptor is open source on GitHub. Agents have moved from answering questions to taking action, and they take action through tools: Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, SaaS APIs, document stores, and web search. Every agent tool call is a data flow. Most enterprise controls cover what goes into and comes out of the model. Far fewer cover what an agent sends to its tools or what those tools send back. That gap shows up in three ways: Patching each agent doesn’t scale across teams and frameworks, and it can’t reach third-party tools. The controls need to sit where every tool call passes, so authorization, content safety, and data protection apply the same way to every agent and tool. AgentCore Gateway is that place. It fronts every tool an agent uses, whatever framework or model the agent runs on. It does more than route that traffic. With AgentCore Gateway interceptors, you can run your own code, as an AWS Lambda function, on every call that passes through it. A request interceptor sees each call before it reaches a tool, and a response interceptor sees each result before it reaches the agent. Either one can inspect the payload, rewrite it, or block the call. That makes the gateway a natural place to add data protection alongside Policy and Guardrails. This single control, attached once, covers every agent and every tool behind the gateway, without any change to agent or tool code. Consider a large European bank with retail and corporate banking operations and strict data-residency obligations. Its operations teams are adopting agents to investigate card disputes. An analyst asks the agent to look into a disputed transaction. The agent searches the web for the merchant, then pulls the dispute case note from Amazon S3 to summarize it. Without protection, three things happen: With the Skyflow interceptor on the gateway, the same workflow plays out differently: The Skyflow interceptor is a single AWS Lambda function attached to both of the AgentCore Gateway interception points: At each point, it calls Skyflow Detect to find sensitive entities such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, government IDs, card numbers, dates of birth, and locations. It replaces them with tokens, or restores the originals. Skyflow Vault stores the original values so authorized systems can reverse the tokens. The Skyflow gateway configuration decides, for each tool, which of three protection modes applies: Shield the tool, Shield the model, and Shield the document. Four properties matter in production: The reference architecture shows where each component sits. The three walkthroughs after it follow a single tool call through the Shield the tool and Shield the document modes. The following diagram shows how the interceptor sits between AgentCore Gateway and your tools. Figure 1: Reference architecture. The numbered steps match the following flow. The agent runs on AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Alongside that flow, the interceptor reads its policy from Parameter Store and its Skyflow API key from Secrets Manager, and it logs each decision to Amazon CloudWatch. It calls Skyflow Detect and Skyflow Vault in an approved Region to de-identify and re-identify data. The targets sit outside the gateway: a third-party web search MCP server, a case-note store in Amazon S3, and a model in Amazon Bedrock that the gateway reaches through an inference target. For model calls, the interceptor keeps a short-lived record in Amazon DynamoDB of which tokens each call minted, so it restores only those. The record holds no original values. For documents, Skyflow Detect fetches the file directly through a presigned URL, so the file bytes never pass through Lambda. This is the web search from the dispute example, step by step. The customer’s name leaves as a token and comes back as the real value, so the search provider never sees it and the analyst still does. Figure 2: Shield the tool. The customer name is replaced with a vault token before the search provider sees the query, and restored before the agent reads the results. This is the analyst asking the agent to draft a reply to the customer. The customer’s name and email address reach the model as tokens, and the draft comes back with the real values in place. Figure 3: Shield the model. The interceptor de-identifies the prompt and the conversation history before the model reads them, and restores the tokens it minted for that call before the agent reads the answer. This is the case-note request. The interceptor never handles the file itself. It checks the presigned URL and hands it to Skyflow Detect, which returns a link to a clean copy. Figure 4: Shield the document. The interceptor checks the presigned URL against the allowlist and size limit, Skyflow Detect fetches and de-identifies the file, and the agent receives a link to the clean copy. Here is the case note as stored in Amazon S3, beside the copy the agent receives: Figure 5: The case note as stored (left) and the de-identified copy the agent receives (right). A token like [NAME_AJbrIud] is a vault token, which an authorized user can reverse through Skyflow. A token like [NAME_1] is a one-way counter that nothing can reverse. The following video shows Shield the document end to end. The agent asks for the dispute case note and receives a link to a de-identified copy instead of the original. Video 1: Shield the document in action. Without Skyflow, the agent reads the original case note. With Skyflow on the gateway, it reads a de-identified copy. The interceptor complements the controls AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock already provide: The Skyflow interceptor is open source in the agentcore-skyflow repository on GitHub under the MIT license. Skyflow is available in AWS Marketplace . To add the interceptor to a gateway you already run: The repository also contains the complete reference deployment from this post, including the agent, the gateway, and its targets, which you can deploy with the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Skyflow offers several vault deployment models and Region choices to meet residency requirements. See Skyflow deployment models . Agents are only as trustworthy as the data they move. With AgentCore Gateway and the Skyflow interceptor, you can enforce a privacy control at the one place every tool call passes through. It works in both directions, covers documents and text, and needs no change to agent code.

title: PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 is now on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
abstract: Dialog-RSN-1, a reasoning model built for real-time complex dialog, is available today on AWS Marketplace and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. It powers frontier dialog: agents that hear a live call, reason about it, and act in real time. As an AWS customer, you can subscribe to Dialog-RSN-1 through AWS Marketplace and deploy it as a SageMaker endpoint inside your own AWS environment. You can also deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker Studio following the steps in Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart . That means the model designed to handle your customer conversations can be deployed like other Amazon SageMaker models with an AWS Marketplace subscription. Dialog-RSN-1 is the first PolyAI model available through AWS Marketplace . It runs inside your own AWS environment on the same AWS cloud that powers PolyAI’s compute and model training and serving. All in a single pass, Dialog-RSN-1 perceives a caller’s audio directly, reasons about what they need, and responds in real time. On SageMaker, it deploys as an endpoint like other models you run there. It is reachable from your own architecture, billed through your AWS account, and covered by the same virtual private cloud (VPC), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and monitoring you already have in place. You keep ownership of orchestration, telephony integration, and business logic. Dialog-RSN-1 takes off your plate the hardest part to build yourself: understanding a live call and responding to it in real time. The endpoint speaks the OpenAI Realtime protocol, so an existing Realtime client connects through PolyAI’s bridge by changing its base URL. Audio in is 16-bit PCM mono at 16 or 24 kHz (transcode G.711 or Opus first). Connections last up to 30 minutes, and the model is English-only today. To get started, find Dialog-RSN-1 on AWS Marketplace , then deploy it straight into an Amazon SageMaker endpoint in your own account. Or you can deploy directly from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart . With Dialog-RSN-1 now onboarded to SageMaker JumpStart, deploying Dialog-RSN-1 takes one click. From the Amazon SageMaker AI console, open the Model Hub, select Dialog-RSN-1 from the JumpStart catalog, and choose Deploy. SageMaker JumpStart then spins up a real-time inference endpoint on a serving stack it has already tuned for you. No containers to wrangle, no instance types to second-guess, and no manual benchmarking. For automated workflows, the same one-click deployment also runs in a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. The Dialog-RSN-1 endpoint runs entirely within your own AWS account. It is deployed in your VPC, accessed through your IAM roles, and monitored with the same Amazon CloudWatch logging and metrics you use for every other workload. Because inference happens inside your account, your callers’ audio and transcripts stay within a boundary you control. For a model handling live customer conversation, this helps support your data residency and auditability requirements. Models built for live calls may make you choose between speed and understanding. And models built for speed may miss the meaning, and ones built for reasoning may lead to wait time for callers. Dialog-RSN-1 avoids the tradeoff. With PolyAI, you can build dialog agents that hear and handle calls the way your human agents would. These agents catch hesitation, hear frustration before it escalates, and know when to speak. Real-time customer conversation is the job PolyAI’s Dialog-RSN-1 is built for, and it is already handling live calls in production today. Because the model reasons directly over the caller’s audio, it picks up tone, hesitation, and timing, the signals a plain transcript loses, and decides for itself the right moment to respond. Dialog-RSN-1 is a model focused on real-time conversations. There is no separate speech-to-text step and no reasoning model on the appropriate moment to talk, so thereby no multiple handoffs. In practice, that means the callers get responses faster: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart is the machine learning hub inside Amazon SageMaker AI, and it exists to collapse the distance between choosing a model and running it in production. For Dialog-RSN-1, that means the frontier of real-time dialog is a few clicks away. You can discover it, prove it on your own data, and ship it to a secure endpoint, all in one place. Here is what you get. Figure 1: The Dialog-RSN-1 model card in SageMaker JumpStart The code path using the SageMaker Python SDK is explained in our GitHub repository: Deploy PolyAI Dialog-RSN-1 on Amazon SageMaker AI . Dialog-RSN-1 shows up in the SageMaker JumpStart catalog with overview and sample notebooks in one place, so your team can understand the model before spending a dollar on infrastructure. To try the model on your own calls, deploy the endpoint and run PolyAI’s sample notebook, which streams recorded caller audio and prints the model’s turn decisions, replies, and transcripts. From the same model card you choose Deploy, and Amazon SageMaker JumpStart stands up a real-time inference endpoint with a pre-configured serving stack. There is no manual container selection or instance guesswork. The real convenience is the named optimization profiles: instead of hand-tuning infrastructure, you pick the target that matches how you run Dialog-RSN-1. Latency optimized minimizes Time to First Token for interactive, real-time calls. Throughput optimized maximizes tokens per second for high call volumes. Cost optimized minimizes infrastructure cost per request. Balanced is an even tradeoff for general-purpose use. Because Dialog-RSN-1 is built to respond in real time, you can use the latency-optimized profile to carry that responsiveness straight to your own endpoint. Before you deploy, SageMaker JumpStart surfaces the key performance metrics: P50 latency, Time to First Token, and throughput. This lets you right-size the ml.* instance for your traffic instead of benchmarking dozens of combinations by hand. You can run the whole flow from the console, or script it through the SageMaker Python SDK to wire deployments into continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD). Figure 2: The Deploy workflow for Dialog-RSN-1 in SageMaker JumpStart Figure 3: Choosing an optimization profile for Dialog-RSN-1 in SageMaker JumpStart The endpoint runs inside your own account boundary: in your VPC, under your IAM roles, with the CloudWatch logging and metrics you already have in place. For a model handling live customer conversations, that means your call audio and transcripts stay in an environment you control, which keeps data residency and auditability straightforward. The result is a frontier voice model that deploys like the other workloads your machine learning team already runs, using the same hub, the same discovery and evaluation tools, and the same security posture. The hard part is the conversation Dialog-RSN-1 handles, not the infrastructure behind it. For more detail on the architecture behind our frontier dialog model and the evaluation results behind our benchmarks, read our Dialog-RSN-1 launch post . Get started today with Dialog-RSN-1 on AWS Marketplace or directly deploy from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart . Also explore SageMaker JumpStart pretrained models .

title: Using NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning on Amazon EKS
abstract: GPU sharing is not new: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), time-slicing, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) address different isolation and utilization needs. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning builds on MPS with Kubernetes-integrated scheduling, per-Pod memory contracts, enforcement, and metrics. NVIDIA Run:ai is AI workload orchestration software for Kubernetes. Its GPU Fractioning Operator can help several teams share one or two GPUs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) . Notebooks, model evaluations, and small inference services can leave teams waiting even when GPU memory remains available. In this walkthrough’s baseline, the NVIDIA device plugin exposes the single GPU as one nvidia.com/gpu resource, with GPU sharing disabled. Two Pods each requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 cannot run concurrently on that node, even when their combined GPU-memory demand fits. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds Kubernetes scheduling integration, enforced GPU-memory limits, and per-Pod metrics to software-based sharing. The approach applies to NVIDIA GPUs that meet the GPU Fractioning Operator’s hardware and software requirements, including GPUs without MIG. We use one Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) g5.xlarge instance with an NVIDIA A10G Tensor Core GPU as the validated example. Other configurations require compatibility checks and validation. NVIDIA announced the open source release of NVIDIA Run:ai on October 13, 2026. This example uses two of its four modular components: KAI Scheduler and GPU Fractioning Operator . KAI Resource Management and Workload Map address organizational governance and additional workload types, outside this walkthrough’s scope. In this post, we show how to build a custom Amazon Linux 2023 (AL2023) image and configure GPU-memory sharing on Amazon EKS. In the validated G5/A10G example, you establish a whole-GPU baseline, give each Pod an 8 GiB memory contract, and verify 6 GiB allocations. You then inspect per-Pod metrics, test rejection of a 9 GiB allocation, and clean up the disposable environment. MIG provides hardware partitions on supported GPUs . Device-plugin time-slicing shares a GPU without replica memory or fault isolation. MPS permits concurrent CUDA processes. Fault containment depends on configuration. NVIDIA Run:ai GPU Fractioning adds enforced per-container memory limits and supports time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing compute modes. NVIDIA documents separate workload error domains for its default mode and a shared error domain for sm-sharing. These are not security guarantees. This walkthrough tests memory limits, not fault containment or compute performance. A memory limit does not reserve proportional compute. Amazon EKS documents several GPU sharing options: MIG , time-slicing with the NVIDIA device plugin , and time-slicing with the NVIDIA DRA driver and Karpenter . For guidance on choosing among them, see the GPU sharing guidance in the Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide. Choose GPU fractioning when you need enforced per-Pod GPU-memory limits on GPUs without MIG and can run fixed-size GPU node groups. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) provides Kubernetes APIs for requesting and allocating devices. GPU sharing and isolation depend on the device driver’s implementation and enabled features. KAI Scheduler and GPU Operator support DRA. This walkthrough uses NvFractions annotations, not DRA. GPU fractioning can help interactive notebooks with idle periods, short evaluation jobs, GPU compatibility tests, and small inference services. Choose each GPU-memory request from measured peak usage plus overhead, then test latency under concurrent load. The demonstrated density improvement does not establish a throughput gain or a universal cost reduction. The following diagram shows the validated single-GPU environment in the US East (Ohio) Region (us-east-2). You use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , eksctl, Helm , and Packer to build and operate it. The Amazon EKS control plane runs Kubernetes version 1.36 in an AWS managed Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) , separate from the customer VPC.
