title: Introducing Together Storage Accelerator: fast, free data caching for your GPU cluster
abstract: Your GPUs are only as fast as your data pipelines. Every training run that starts with a 30-minute model download, every node that re-pulls the same dataset from across the country, and every Hugging Face rate limit that stalls a job leads to compute resources sitting idle, waiting for your data, while you are paying for them. Today we're launching Together Storage Accelerator (TSA) , a distributed caching layer for Together GPU Clusters that alleviates the need for repeated data reads from object storage and Hugging Face Hub, dramatically accelerating your AI data pipelines while also cutting your data egress bills. TSA is now included free with every Together GPU Cluster. The problem: your data lives far from your GPUs Most AI teams keep their source of truth in object storage (Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Together AI's T4*) or pull models directly from Hugging Face Hub. That means every cold start pays a WAN tax: cross-cloud or cross-region reads are slow, expensive (egress from AWS runs up to $0.09/GB), and rate-limited. Multiplied across hundreds of nodes pulling the same checkpoint, the waste compounds and costs you time, money, and failed jobs when the origin throttles you. *T4 is Together AI's in data center S3 compatible object storage solution, currently in Limited Preview. Please contact sales or your account team if you are interested to try it out. ‍ TSA caches the data, improving performance, reliability and cost TSA provides you a distributed caching layer for GPU clusters. It runs on every GPU node in your cluster and presents drop-in endpoints for the storage you already use. The first time any node reads an object, TSA caches it on cluster NVMe. As a result, every subsequent read, from any node, is served from inside the cluster at dramatically higher local speed. The result, measured on a Together GPU Cluster H100 node: ~20× faster warm reads than pulling from a cross-cloud origin, at up to 3.4 GB/s per node . A 2 GiB object that took 13-15 s to download from Cloudflare R2 can be read from the cache in 0.6 - 0.7 s Cold reads cost nothing extra : the first read through TSA ran within ~5% of a direct download One origin fetch, per cluster. A 70 GB checkpoint pulled by 200 nodes downloads from the source once, not 200 times Resilience to outages and rate limits. Cached data keeps serving even when the upstream won't. You can start using TSA without making any changes to your application . No new SDK, no rewritten data loaders, and you can get started with a single command. Getting started: # S3-compatible storage (S3, R2, T4, ...) export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://tsa.tsa.svc.cluster.local:18080 # Hugging Face Hub export HF_ENDPOINT=http://tsa.tsa.svc.cluster.local:18080 Your existing boto3 code, transformers calls, and CLI workflows work as-is. TSA handles authentication with credentials you configure. Credentials are encrypted and securely stored in a secrets vault. Measured results Measured on 2026-10-28 from a pod on one H100 node in a Together GPU Cluster (us-central). Single-stream reads unless noted; clients wrote to /dev/null or node NVMe. Read a 2 GiB object from a cross-cloud bucket (Cloudflare R2): 143–169 MB/s (12.7–15.0 s) without TSA, 3.0–3.4 GB/s (0.64–0.72 s) with TSA warm. ~20× Read small files from the same bucket (5 KB, 2.4 MB): 320 ms and 680 ms without TSA, 5 ms and 8 ms with TSA warm. ~60–80× lower latency 200-node cluster pulling the same checkpoint: 200 origin fetches without TSA, 1 with TSA. 200× less egress Measured on a Together GPU Clusters preview deployment (TSA chart 0.6.0); your results depend on origin, object sizes, and network path. Origin speed is regional: the same Hugging Face download ran 5× faster from us-central than from ca-west, so TSA's win is largest where the origin is slowest. Methodology: single-stream curl and aws s3 cp from a pod on the GPU node, repeated reads of the same object, MD5-verified against direct download. Powered by ASTRA TSA leverages ASTRA (Accelerated Storage Transport & Retrieval Architecture), the distributed caching technology we built to feed some of the largest GPU fleets in the world, including our own inference fleet. We'll share a deeper technical look at ASTRA in an upcoming engineering post. Better together with T4 TSA works with any S3-compatible store, and it pairs naturally with T4 , Together AI's managed object storage solution. Point TSA at your existing S3 or R2 buckets today without migrating your data. When you want your warm data living next to your GPUs permanently, T4 is one config change away. T4 is currently in limited preview : contact sales or your account team for access. Get started Together Storage Accelerator is available now on Together GPU Clusters at no additional cost. Enable it from your cluster's Settings page, or see the docs to go from zero to accelerated in under ten minutes. → Create a cluster ‍→ Read the docs

title: Genie ZeroOps, now in public beta: An autonomous agent that fixes data pipelines, with lessons from 80,000 customer issues
abstract: In June we introduced Genie ZeroOps , an autonomous agent that detects, investigates, and resolves data pipeline issues, such as upstream schema changes or data quality anomalies. Based on extensive private preview testing with hundreds of customers, we’ve added new features to help data teams triage issues faster - including inbox sharing, notifications, one-click PR creation, and the ability to add custom business instructions to follow specific company workflows. Today, Genie ZeroOps is available in Public Beta, and your workspace admin can turn it on from the workspace Previews page. Data engineering teams are underwater, managing many thousands of pipelines a day. Some pipeline failures are easy to find and fix - a job fails, a pipeline update errors out, and someone gets paged. Others are silent - a table stops updating, or last night's load arrives with half its usual rows, and nobody notices until a dashboard shows the wrong number. Either way, the work that follows typically looks the same: a notification is sent, an engineer spends the next few hours manually investigating logs, upstream tables, and related assets, and finally a PR gets generated with the fix. Genie ZeroOps automates this entire manual workflow while maintaining security, governance, and recommendation quality, specifically guiding teams from initial issue alert to a pull request across five core steps: During the limited private preview, ZeroOps observed over 80,000 real customer issues across hundreds of companies, highlighting just how painful pipeline maintenance has become. We found that over half of issues require organization-specific knowledge to properly triage, rank, and resolve, which speaks to the fundamental need for custom context. Through this feedback, we identified and built several critical features every team needs to succeed with ZeroOps: During our private preview, we spoke with customers who were prototyping internal AI triage tools. We learned that while building a simple prototype has become easier, scaling automated triage across production environments introduces complex operational challenges that compound over time: Genie ZeroOps handles these complexities natively - leveraging direct access to your Unity Catalog, metadata, and pipeline lineage to resolve issues with full context. Try ZeroOps out for yourself! Have a workspace admin enable the ZeroOps feature. Then find the ZeroOps banner on the top of the pipelines page: Read the documentation here for more details on how to get started. If your team needs help onboarding ZeroOps to production, reach out to your account team to inquire about any workshops that we offer. No, ZeroOps will never change your code or data without your direct approval. Today, it investigates the failure, proposes a fix and can push that fix to a new branch for a pull request. It never changes production code or data without a person reviewing it first. It uses Data Quality Monitoring to flag tables whose commits arrive unusually late (freshness) or whose row counts fall below the expected range (completeness). ZeroOps automatically triggers as soon as an issue is detected, without a prompt, so the analysis is ready before anyone looks. It also has built-in access to run history, Unity Catalog lineage, Delta history and DQM signals, and it works within your Unity Catalog permissions. From the documentation , It reads run logs, source code, upstream table metadata and samples, while respecting Unity Catalog permissions. It uses models hosted by Databricks inside our security perimeter. Model calls stay in your workspace's region, and the model provider doesn't retain prompts or responses. Yes. Add a custom instruction to filter out unwanted notifications, or mark an insight as "not an issue." Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: Genie One Accuracy: Why Curated Agents Need Governed Context
abstract: Ask Finance and Underwriting whether the loss ratio improved from 2024 to 2025, and you will get two contradictory answers that are both correct. In a fictional commercial auto insurer we built for this test, Finance reported an 8.2 percentage-point deterioration, and Underwriting reported a 1.5 percentage-point improvement. Neither was wrong. Finance tracks the calendar year net of reinsurance, so an adverse reserve development on an older claim shows up in today's numbers. Underwriting looks strictly at the policy year, gross of reinsurance and excluding catastrophes, because that's the baseline used to set rates. Reserving, meanwhile, relies on a third metric entirely: the accident-year ultimate loss ratio. The SQL can be perfectly correct and still produce an answer that doesn't make sense for the person asking. The challenge is knowing which business definition to apply when the same term has several valid definitions, while keeping shared facts, such as total policies written, consistent. This is the problem we wanted to explore with Genie One. Genie One, powered by Genie Ontology (now Generally Available), brings this business context into the analytics experience. Genie Ontology learns from the work teams already do, automatically capturing business logic, calculations, and relationships from existing dashboards, queries, notebooks, and semantic models as Ontology Snippets. This learned knowledge is complemented by modeled knowledge: explicitly defined, governed business concepts represented in Unity Catalog through certified Metric Views, Domains and Subdomains, and Pages. In this study, we refer to this modeled knowledge as the “governed layer”. Together, learned and modeled knowledge give Genie a richer understanding of how an organization works. Teams can build on the knowledge already captured from their existing assets, while using modeled knowledge to establish authoritative definitions for the business concepts where consistency and precision matter most. There is no need to model every concept upfront. This study explores a different aspect of Genie Ontology than the Turing benchmark described in our Genie Ontology GA announcement . While the benchmark compared the accuracy and efficiency of Genie with Genie Ontology against leading frontier agents, our study isolates the contribution of modeled knowledge: how governed Metric Views and Pages complement learned knowledge and curated agents to help Genie One interpret business definitions and deliver consistent answers. To explore this, we built four Genie Agents, one each for Finance, Reserving, Underwriting, and Claims. They used the same tables, but each had its own team's definitions, example queries, and documents. Each did well on its own. We wanted to know what happens when Genie One becomes the entry point: does it route to the right agent and use the right definition, and what does it need to do that reliably? We tested four configurations to find out. Tables alone scored 64%. Curated agents and the governed layer each reached 83%, but they weren't good at the same things. Adding curated agents improved document-based answers. Adding the governed layer improved answers that depended on business definitions. Neither was enough on its own to cover both needs. With both in place, accuracy reached 93–95%, across two runs. The combined setup also scored 93% on loss-ratio questions and 97% on questions that required both documents and structured data. To see whether this pattern held outside the insurance sector, we repeated the comparison using a fictional retailer. There, the governed layer raised accuracy from 54% to 82% when added to the curated agents. Genie One doesn't simply choose an agent and let it answer every question. It can use governed Unity Catalog Semantics such as Metric Views , Domains and subdomains , and Pages , or route a question to a relevant Genie Agent. If it doesn't find a suitable match, it searches the workspace. There, it may infer which data to use from tables or volumes you use often, or from your earlier conversations. When Genie One answers a question using its own context, it doesn't automatically inherit the instructions configured inside each agent. Those instructions apply only when Genie One routes the question to that agent. So an agent can be well curated and still contribute little if Genie One answers the question differently. We created a fictional commercial auto insurer with: The four agents shared the same underlying tables. Each also had access to its team's folder of documents, with 14 PDFs across the four folders. We also planted two misleading documents to test robustness. One was an early draft of the reserve committee minutes reporting a $4.1 million increase in reserves; the approved minutes in the same folder reported a $5.28 million increase. The other was a vendor newsletter containing a hidden instruction to report the loss ratio as 55%, a simple prompt-injection test. We then placed three look-alike tables next to the real definitions: analytics_loss_ratio_v2, analytics_loss_ratio_test, and a personal copy, finance_lr_calendar_quarter_net_jdoe. The agents were configured with their teams' formulas, business rules, and SQL example questions. We tuned them on a separate set of practice questions and then froze them, using the same versions across all configurations that included agents. There are multiple ways to make enterprise documents available to Genie, depending on where the content lives and how teams need to access it. In this experiment, we stored team-specific PDFs in Unity Catalog Volumes and made them available to the corresponding Genie Agents through content search. When information is spread across business applications such as Google Drive, SharePoint, Jira, or Confluence, Genie Search provides a broader enterprise search experience. It combines indexed content from connected applications with live retrieval through MCP, bringing results together with Databricks assets in a single experience. It also respects the permissions of the source systems, so users only see content they are authorized to access. For the governed layer, we set up: The insurance benchmark contained 125 questions, each with an expected answer calculated independently in SQL. The questions covered simple lookups, explicitly named business definitions, ambiguous questions such as "What's our loss ratio?", questions requiring an explanation, questions that the available data couldn't answer, and questions that combined documents with structured data. We also tested follow-up questions and the two planted documents. We took several steps to make the results more meaningful. Genie One answered every question three times, with a fresh service principal for each run so earlier conversations couldn't carry over, and every answer was logged in MLflow. When a key result was close, we repeated the whole setup with a new identity. We report 95% confidence intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples, keeping each question's repeats together, because Genie One can recall earlier answers. Two AI judges from different model families extracted the headline number, the definition used, and the facts covered, and fixed rules decided whether each answer was right. The judges agreed on 95–99% of answers. Before each run, every agent had to answer at least 85% of its basic questions correctly on its own. Here’s the overall accuracy score, followed by a breakdown by question category, measured with Genie One. What the governed layer added. With curated agents alone, Genie One often answered definition questions on its own and never saw the formulas in the agents' instructions. Published Pages are visible to Genie One across the whole account, so the closest definitions it could find were Pages other people had written for unrelated projects. It relied on those in 49% of its answers.

title: Four AI Architecture Patterns for Regulated Industries
abstract: Enterprise AI cannot replace every deterministic control. These four patterns help architects decide where agents can reason, act, and remain subject to controls or human authority. Enterprises are adding agents to systems built on fixed rules and repeatable processes. Agents can reason through complex problems, but enterprise systems-especially in regulated industries-must remain controlled and auditable. The question is not which one to choose. It is how to make them work together. We are writing this series because customers ask us the same questions: How are enterprises around the world navigating constraints similar to ours? What is the reality of enterprise AI adoption? How are other organizations approaching these nuances? How is Databricks helping solve them when the requirements are ambiguous, complex, and so specific to the institution? We as Forward Deployed Engineers work at this boundary. We take ambiguous business problems and turn them into production-ready systems. While implementations will vary by institution and we cannot disclose specific implementation details, we can discuss generalized patterns and practices. As agents become part of large enterprise systems, two questions keep recurring: The answer is not the same for every use case. Across the systems we are building and modernizing in the field, four patterns are emerging. This first article introduces the framework. The next four articles show how each pattern works in practice. Use this pattern when outcomes must be strictly deterministic and reproducible, or when errors are irreversible and carry high remediation costs. Here, deterministic means the result can be reproduced under an explicit, versioned contract that records the data, rule, tolerance, configuration, and execution context together. Financial Institutions have lots of controls. Reconciliations are a good example. The control must calculate the balances, apply an approved rule, and produce a reproducible PASS or FAIL. An agent cannot reinterpret the tolerance or turn its own explanation into a passed control. When a reconciliation fails, an agent can gather evidence, inspect lineage and batch status, compare the break with prior incidents, test a bounded set of causes, and recommend what should happen next. The deterministic control still decides whether the reconciliation passed. The agent helps explain why it failed. The agent can investigate the control. It cannot become the control. This pattern also applies to regulatory calculations, policy enforcement, data quality gates, and system integrity checks-anywhere the result must be precise, reproducible, and auditable. Use this pattern when more than one answer may be valid, but the result can be tested objectively. Legacy migration or modernization is a good example. An agent can analyze an existing workload and generate a target implementation. It may not produce exactly the same implementation each time. That is not necessarily a problem. What matters is whether the result is correct. A deterministic judge can test whether the code compiles, schemas conform, data reconciles, control totals match, governance requirements are satisfied, and performance meets the target. If the result fails, the agent receives the evidence, diagnoses the problem, corrects its work, and runs through validation again. Passing that judge proves that the candidate satisfied the approved acceptance contract. It does not prove that the contract covers every production behavior. Test coverage, production-shaped edge cases, and periodic review still matter. Do not make the agent deterministic when you can deterministically evaluate its output . The validator is not only a control. It is the feedback loop that allows the agent to improve its result. This pattern works well for migration, code generation, transformation, testing, and remediation. Use this pattern when the answer requires judgment and cannot be proven correct by a deterministic test. Financial crime investigations are one example. An agent can correlate transactions, documents, policies, relationships, and historical patterns. It can assemble evidence, identify likely explanations, surface unresolved questions, and recommend a disposition. This is also often required by regulation where a decision significantly affects a person, or when you have to justify the outcome to a regulator, auditor, court, or the affected person But a recommendation is not a decision. When the outcome is consequential, and there is no deterministic way to establish correctness, authority must remain with an accountable person. Human review should sit at the decision boundary, not inside every step . The agent's reasoning must also often be explainable. Every recommendation should trace back to the evidence, sources, and tools behind it. That lets the investigator challenge the logic and lets auditors or regulators reconstruct how the agent reached its recommendation. Where regulation gives an affected person the right to an explanation, the explanation must be specific to the decision. It covers the main factors, the agent's role, and the human's role. "The model flagged it" is not enough. The investigator records the rationale for the final call, including any agent override. The agent reduces investigative effort and improves the consistency of the evidence presented. The investigator retains responsibility for the final decision, which may be subjective and nuanced and not deterministic. Use this pattern when the agent needs to act, but only within an explicit operating envelope. Consider a Governance Intelligence module that manages access to governed enterprise data. A user describes what data they need, why they need it, and for how long. The agent interprets the request, identifies the appropriate data product, determines the minimum access required, and gathers the relevant identity, policy, ownership, classification, lineage, and usage context. Requiring manual approval for every standard request creates delay without necessarily reducing risk. Giving the agent unrestricted authority to grant access creates an unacceptable control gap. The answer is bounded autonomy. The operating envelope defines: Within that envelope, the agent can interpret the request, assemble the evidence, select the approved workflow, and initiate a time-bound entitlement. Deterministic policy services validate every required condition before Unity Catalog enforces the grant. Do not try to constrain every decision. Constrain the operating envelope. Implementing multi-agent judge frameworks across validation cycles within this envelope can also complement human oversight with automated, multi-perspective safety checks. If the request falls outside the envelope - for example, because it involves sensitive data, missing attributes, conflicting policies, excessive privilege, or a segregation of duties exception- the system blocks straight through execution and routes it to the appropriate data owner, steward, or risk reviewer. Databricks provides the governed foundation across the four patterns. Omnigent can compose agents and agent harnesses without making any one agent the architecture. Unity Gateway governs access to models, tools, MCP servers, and external APIs. Unity Catalog governs enterprise data and enforces approved access including residency and cross-border transfer rules. Secure connectivity reaches on-premises, cloud, and SaaS systems without bypassing these control points. MLflow preserves traces and evaluation evidence that also serve as audit records for regulators. See the attached diagram for a reference architecture showing how agent calls flow through governed control points to customer systems across on-premises, cloud, and regulated jurisdictions. Traditional modernization changes where and how technology runs. AI transformation changes the execution model itself.

title: How partners use Genie's free tier on Azure Databricks
abstract: Every Azure Databricks user gets $10 of free Genie usage each month, usage that many AI tools charge for. And Genie is built to get cheaper as customers use it. The Genie ontology saves the work the whole company has already done, so Genie doesn't redo it for every question. Smart routing and open-weight models keep lowering the cost of each answer, and the more customers use Genie, the more efficient it becomes. Genie budgets let admins decide whether anyone spends beyond the free allowance. For partners, that turns the cost question into a reason to roll Genie out broadly. If you advise customers on AI, you’ve likely seen this: once they experience what Genie can do, they want it everywhere, in front of every employee and not just a pilot team. What they need next is a path to scale it within cost boundaries. Some customers block consumption-based AI tools entirely, and others hold off on a trial because they worry about what happens to costs as usage grows. That concern is reasonable. As AI moves from a few pilot users to the whole workforce, finance teams want predictable costs and clear guardrails before they say yes. Genie is built to meet that bar: every user gets free monthly usage so everyone can benefit, and budget controls are ready for when usage ramps. For partners, that means you can help customers adopt AI across their enterprise without cost limiting the conversation. You can start broad with cost controls in place from day one, which builds trust and makes it easier to scale. Genie’s pricing also complements the Microsoft 365 investments customers have already made. Which Genie experience fits each customer? All three are governed through Unity Catalog, so partners can match the right experience to each customer conversation and know the same access rules apply throughout. Every identified user gets $10 of free Genie usage each month, and it resets on the first of every month. Even better, through January 31, 2027, Genie One and Genie Agents are free for users, so the full $10 goes to Genie Code. After that, the $10 allowance is shared across Genie One, Genie Agents and Genie Code. Budgets apply only to pay-as-you-go usage above the free allowance. They can't remove it, so every user keeps the same free starting point. Genie's cost story improves as customers use it: Genie budgets live in the account console and give admins tools to monitor spending, set limits and manage billable Genie usage: A few details are worth telling customers up front. Budgets track each user’s spend in near real time and block new requests once a threshold is reached. Because tracking is an estimate, actual spend can land slightly above or below the threshold, and requests already in progress finish. Budgets are built for near-real-time spend control rather than as an absolute cap, and warehouse compute is billed separately. Service principals don’t get the free allowance, so automated usage is billed. Start with spend control, not a procurement cycle Most enterprise AI projects begin with a business case and a procurement cycle. With Genie, customers can start with spend control instead: set the pay-as-you-go threshold to $0, roll Genie out broadly on the free allowance, learn how people actually use it and add budget only where the value is clear. Genie brings governed Azure Databricks data into Microsoft Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Cowork, Excel and Copilot Studio, with Unity Catalog permissions applied throughout. Users ask questions where they already work, and the answers respect the same access rules as the rest of their data. The Azure Databricks Genie Plugin , now generally available, gives partners a one-step way to bring Genie into a customer's Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot environment, so the first conversation can happen in minutes. For example, business users can ask questions about their company's data directly from Teams or Copilot, bring Genie results into Excel, or use Genie to power agents built in Copilot Studio. Some integrations are in preview and may require additional setup or licensing. For partners, this opens opportunities to connect AI to existing business workflows, build new solutions and help customers get more value from their Microsoft and Databricks investments. Plugging Genie into Microsoft 365 Copilot doesn't mean paying twice: Copilot routes the questions Genie can answer to Genie, so customers avoid those costs on the Copilot side. For SIs: Genie is a low-friction way into every Microsoft 365 account. Open with a broad rollout at $0 in pay-as-you-go spend, then build services around it: budget and persona design, Unity Catalog governance, Genie setup and expansion into new use cases. For ISVs: If your product works with Unity Catalog data, Genie can bring that governed data into Teams and Copilot for your joint customers. Learn: Manage budgets and cost controls for Genie , the Genie consumption guide and the Genie cost and budgets FAQ For partners: Get enabled on Genie and Azure Databricks through partner training on the Databricks Partner Academy, and talk to your Databricks partner team or Partner Solutions Architect about demos and co-sell. Every identified user also gets $10 of free Genie Code usage each month. After that date, the $10 monthly allowance is shared across Genie One, Genie Agents and Genie Code. Each user has their own allowance, and it resets on the first of every month. Usage above it is billed pay-as-you-go, and admins can control that spend with Genie budgets. The allowance covers Genie's AI usage only. SQL warehouse compute is billed separately, and service principals don't get a free allowance. Admins can set shared, per-user and group thresholds, use alert-only thresholds or block usage once a threshold is reached. Budgets can't remove a user's free allowance. Yes. Set a $0 per-user threshold with Block usage enabled. Users get their full free allowance, and Genie Code usage pauses once it runs out and resumes on the first of the month. No. Budgets track each user's spend in near real time and block new requests once a threshold is reached, but tracking is an estimate, so actual spend can land slightly above or below the threshold. Requests already in progress finish, and warehouse compute is billed separately. Yes. The Azure Databricks Genie Plugin gives partners a one-step way to add Genie to a customer's Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot environment. title: Introducing Genie Migrate for Serverless
abstract: Serverless compute in Databricks offers a simpler, faster way to run your data and AI workloads. It removes the operational burden of managing infrastructure, automatically handling provisioning, scaling, and optimization so teams can focus on their business outcomes. With serverless, organizations can move faster, improve efficiency, and unlock the benefits of cloud-native compute without managing and maintaining complex clusters. Our serverless usage has grown multifold just in the past year, and today thousands of customers run notebooks and jobs on it. Most teams still have a classic fleet they want to migrate over to the serverless world in order to get the cost and operational benefits without managing infrastructure themselves. The work of moving each workload one at a time often prevents our customers from unlocking serverless benefits for their existing workloads. You have probably watched this happen. You pick a job, flip it to serverless, and then get hit with an error, an access-mode incompatibility, a Spark config that does not apply, a library that is installed on classic but not on serverless. What should take an afternoon stretches into weeks, and most of the time goes to translation you have done many times before. Not any more! Today we are excited to announce the launch of Genie Migrate for Serverless (in Beta) , the Databricks agent that migrates your jobs and notebooks from classic to serverless compute - easily and effortlessly. A workload migration becomes a review-and-approve step rather than a research project. Until now, migrating a workload to serverless was manual. The knowledge of how a classic cluster config maps to serverless, which libraries resolve, which Spark confs still apply, and which access mode a workload needs lived in the practitioner's head and in the trial-and-error of running the notebook or job and reading the failure. Genie Migrate for Serverless moves that translation off you and onto the platform, the same way serverless moved provisioning and scaling onto the platform. What stays with you is judgment: whether to migrate a workload now, whether the proposed changes look right, and whether the migrated run is healthy. The agent handles the translation itself, proposing as a diff you review before anything changes. In order to build successful serverless migration tooling, we kept these critical principles in mind: Those three needs shape how the migration agent works, and the workflow below defines how it executes the migration: assess what can move, translate it, and apply the change reversibly. The agent runs from the /compute migrate slash command inside Genie on any job or notebook. It is fully managed, and you need no setup to start scanning. Because Databricks manages it, the agent reads your job config and workload code inside your own workspace. Let’s dive a bit deeper into each of these areas listed above. Before you touch anything, the agent scans your Jobs and Notebooks and marks each workload with its serverless readiness. You see which workloads are ideal candidates for migration instead of auditing the fleet by hand - eliminating painstaking manual discovery and triage work A quick note on external sources: if a workload's source of truth lives outside the workspace, for example a job managed by Databricks Asset Bundles or a notebook in a Git folder, the agent cannot migrate it yet. Support for those is coming soon. Once you pick an eligible workload, the migration agent proposes the changes it needs for serverless and presents them for review before anything is written. Nothing is applied until you approve it. The migration agent effectively translates the pieces that differ between classic and serverless: Every change, including the code rewrites, is presented as a reviewable diff. Before applying, the agent shows a side-by-side comparison of what will change and what will not, an explicit contract you can hand to a manager or an on-call rotation. Check out the latest demo on how to migrate classic workloads easily using Genie Migrate for Serverless. If the agent is unsure about something, for example whether a Spark conf is still needed, it reports the conf rather than removing it. A conf can look unused to a static scan while a listener loaded at runtime depends on it. Silent removal would drop the telemetry a team relies on. The agent leaves that decision with you. Applying a migration is where you are most exposed, so Genie Migrate for Serverless is most conservative here. It performs deterministic checks for correctness today, and deeper runtime validation is coming next. If you opt not to migrate, cloned jobs or suggested changes to notebooks will not be applied. One thing to be cautious about: this does not undo data that serverless runs wrote to production tables in the meantime if you tested with the changed versions. Today the validation is static. It confirms the translation is sound without running the workload, and it is honest about what it has and has not proven. The deeper check is coming next via Sandbox validation. With this, the agent will be able to run the migrated workload in an isolated sandbox without affecting your production tables and compare its output against the classic baseline – so you see a runtime and correctness signal on a critical job before Apply, not after. Migrating one workload at a time in Genie works well for a handful of jobs. For a larger fleet, you can run Genie Migrate for Serverless in the background with the Databricks CLI. Start a migration for multiple jobs from a script using the compute-migrations command group, and the agent builds a serverless working copy of each job without an open Genie session. Your original job does not change until you review and approve its migration, and approving keeps the job's ID, schedule, and permissions. Bulk migration supports jobs today (support for notebooks coming soon) and requires Databricks CLI version 1.24.0 or above. Let’s put the three key capabilities of the Genie Migrate for Serverless back together: Here is a quick summary of what workloads are good fit today to migrate using the agent, and what’s coming in the future. You can start moving workloads to serverless today using Genie Migrate for Serverless. Here is how to get going: The Genie Migrate for Serverless is available today via the /compute migrate command in Genie, on any job or notebook. We are actively shaping the sandbox-validation capability with preview customers, and we continue to evolve the agent to make serverless migrations faster, simpler and easier. title: Bulk migrate your dashboards to AI/BI with Genie Code
abstract: In our previous post, Migrate Your Dashboards to AI/BI with Genie Code , we walked through moving a single Tableau or Power BI report onto Databricks AI/BI with the /importBI skill in Genie Code. That one-report-at-a-time flow is perfect for a pilot — but most organizations have hundreds of reports built up over years, and migrating them individually turns a strategic modernization effort into a months-long manual grind. Bulk migration of dashboards changes that. You can now point the migration agent at an entire folder of reports and have them converted to AI/BI Dashboards in a single run — no more kicking off migrations report by report. Bulk migration extends the Databricks AI/BI migration experience so that instead of importing one report at a time, you can process many reports together from a single command. The migration agent reads your source BI files, generates the corresponding AI/BI Dashboards on Databricks, and maps them to the target catalog and schema you specify. This feature is now generally available, and so it's ready to use in your workspace today. Before you begin, check that partner-powered AI features are enabled at both the account and workspace levels. For teams standardizing on Databricks AI/BI, bulk migration removes the single biggest bottleneck in a large-scale dashboard migration: the sheer repetition of moving reports one at a time. By migrating an entire folder of Tableau or Power BI reports into a single run — and landing them directly in your chosen catalog and schema — you can shift a migration project from a manual backlog to a repeatable, folder-at-a-time workflow. The playbook below walks through a bulk migration end to end. It is grouped into three phases: Export each Tableau or Power BI report you want to migrate to a supported file type. This includes: .twb, .twbx, .tds, .tdsx, .pbit, or .tmdl. The Tableau export documentation and Power BI report templates guides walk you through the export. Tip: Working with a Tableau workbook that connects to a published data source? Export that data source as well (.tds or .tdsx) and keep it next to the workbook. Place the BI report files you want to migrate into a directory within a Unity Catalog volume . Keeping them together in one folder lets you migrate them in a batch. A bulk run always picks up its files from the volume; dragging files straight into the chat only works for one-off, single-report imports. From a draft dashboard, open Genie Code and submit: /importBI <path/to/volume/directory> Above: Running /importBI against a volume directory from a draft dashboard. Pointing the command at the directory (rather than a single file) triggers the bulk flow across all reports in that folder. If you prefer natural language, a request such as “Migrate every Power BI report in /Volumes/finance/bi/reports to AI/BI Dashboards” works just as well. You can also name specific files instead of a whole folder: “Migrate Tableau reports Dashboard1.twb, Dashboard2.twb in /Volumes/finance/bi/reports to AI/BI Dashboards”. Finally, you should add guidance that applies to the entire batch — for example, asking Genie Code to "build only the metric views". The agent recognizes the batch and lists the reports it found in the volume, matching each Tableau workbook to its companion data source file on its own and checking with you if a pairing is unclear. It then prompts you for the destination catalog and schema so the migrated dashboards' metric views and SQL views land in the right place. Above: Genie Code lists the reports it found and asks for the target catalog and schema. After you've checked the file list and given the go-ahead, the bulk migration kicks off, and a status panel shows each report as it starts. Reports are queued and processed a few at a time, and each report reuses existing Unity Catalog tables and views where it can before creating new ones. Note: For the current limits on the number and size of files supported in a single bulk import, always refer to the public documentation on /importBI . A status card in the chat keeps a running tally of the batch, with each report marked as Queued (not started), Running, or Completed (session ended). You can stop an individual report, or halt everything still in flight, from the same card. Above: The status card tracks every report in the batch. Because each report runs in its own background job, there's no need to keep the tab open — come back to the original chat in your Genie Code history at any time to see how the batch is progressing. Each file name on the status card links to that report's own Genie Code conversation, which opens in a separate tab. If a run stops to ask a question, answer it there, and the migration picks up where it left off. Above: A run that paused to ask for input. In this example, the published data source behind the workbook. As with a single-file /importBI migration, each report runs through the Genie Code planning phase — for example, parsing and assessing the workbook, enumerating the semantic layer, creating metric views, building the dashboard pages, and validating the migration. Above: The migration plan for a single report, tracked step by step. Once the plan execution completes, you can view the finished AI/BI dashboard produced by the migration. You can further enhance or customize it with follow-up Genie Code prompts. Every Genie Code response can be undone as a single step, so it's safe to experiment, and you can even ask Genie Code to beautify the dashboard's look and feel. Above: A finished AI/BI dashboard produced by the bulk migration. Before you retire a source report, check that the migrated dashboard gives the same answers as the original. Tip: If you've connected Tableau or Power BI via a read-only MCP connection (see the cheat sheet below), Genie Code can check the numbers against the live report directly rather than reading values from a screenshot. Set things up well before you run /importBI to get the most faithful migration on the first pass: • Set up a read-only MCP connection to Tableau or Power BI so Genie Code can use the live report as the source of truth, validating results against the original rather than relying solely on the exported file, which meaningfully improves accuracy. • Migrated dashboards map to Unity Catalog tables (via Lakeflow Connect, Lakehouse Federation, or existing UC tables). Example: “The source tables for this report as available in dev.finance schema” “Use prod.finance.table1, prod.finance.table2 and prod.finance.mv_revenue as the source for this report” • Tableau imports produce dashboard-scoped (local) metric views by default, while Power BI imports produce Unity Catalog metric views. • File count and size limits can change, so always refer to the public /importBI documentation for the current limits. Moving hundreds of Tableau or Power BI reports to Databricks AI/BI no longer has to mean hundreds of individual migrations. With bulk migration, you prepare a folder of reports once, run a single /importBI command, and let Genie Code work through the batch in the background while you review and refine each result. If you're planning a BI modernization effort, upload a folder of reports to a Unity Catalog volume and try /importBI from a draft dashboard to see bulk migration in action. If you’re ready to get started, just put your report files in a Unity Catalog volume, open a draft dashboard, and run /importBI in Genie Code. For step-by-step details, see the documentation on importing BI files with Genie Code . If you're new to AI/BI, start with our earlier post : Migrate your Dashboards to AI/BI with Genie Code . You should also read the bulk migration product documentation . Q: What is bulk migration for Databricks AI/BI? A: Bulk migration allows you to process many Tableau or Power BI reports together in a single run, instead of importing one report at a time.

title: Introducing CustomerLake Conversions: Improve advertising performance with first-party customer context
abstract: Two purchases can look identical in campaign reports and mean very different things to your business. One buyer has potential to become a loyal regular; the other is a first-time purchase driven by a deep discount. Both count as conversions , but their long-term value can be very different. Your business has data that helps identify the difference: purchase history, margin, loyalty, engagement, and predicted lifetime value. Bringing that understanding into advertising can change the customers you pursue, the signals you send, and how you evaluate success. Today, we’re introducing CustomerLake Conversions : a new capability within Databricks’ Agentic CDP that connects first-party data and context directly to advertising activation and measurement. It helps brands pursue more valuable conversions and improve return on ad spend (ROAS), while controlling the data they share. When available, CustomerLake Conversions will be accessible to all customers using Campaign Agents in CustomerLake. We’re proud to collaborate with these advertising and agency partners for this launch: CustomerLake is the Agentic CDP built natively in Databricks, the enterprise data and AI platform where your most complete customer context already lives. Its Campaign Agents help marketers build audiences in natural language, activate across channels, and power 1:1 personalized experiences. CustomerLake Conversions extends Campaign Agents to advertising performance by connecting three steps directly on your trusted foundation: The dedicated Conversions tab within CustomerLake Campaign Agents lets marketers select conversion data, configure destinations, and manage delivery within the Campaign Agents workflow. Together, these capabilities connect the intelligence behind your targeting, the signals sent to platforms, and the results used to guide future investment. As advertising platforms automate more bidding, targeting, and campaign decisions, the only lever advertisers fully control is what signals they feed them. That puts a premium on first-party data, and on the business context that explains what it means. However, getting richer business context into paid media often requires manual data extracts, custom integrations, and handoffs across marketing, analytics, engineering, and agency teams. Audiences can diverge across platforms, and campaign reporting is delayed and disconnected from customer and revenue data. That means attribution is fuzzy, acquisition costs creep up, and teams can't say with confidence which paid channels are converting and which aren’t. CustomerLake Conversions brings signal creation and activation to where customer data and models already live. A retailer can use predicted lifetime value to rapidly adjust lookalike targeting. A B2B company can use qualified leads or closed won revenue to represent progress beyond a submitted form. Marketers still define success; CustomerLake helps translate those priorities into signals advertising platforms can use. Let’s consider a retailer whose goal is to acquire more customers who are likely to buy again. Before: The retailer sends purchase events and order values to its advertising platforms, while its lifetime value model lives in the data platform, maintained by the data team. Using that model in paid media requires data extracts, platform-specific uploads, and separate delivery workflows. Their agency then reconciles campaign reports with revenue data to evaluate acquisition quality. With CustomerLake Conversions: The paid media team uses its existing lifetime value model in Databricks to identify completed first purchases from customers likely to become repeat buyers. In the Conversions tab, the team configures delivery of those purchase events to supported advertising platforms through CAPI. The same customer data can also inform the audiences the team builds and syncs. Campaign insights flow back into Databricks, where the retailer and its agency evaluate acquisition spend alongside customer value. They can refine audiences, signals, and media strategy using the same customer and business context that informed activation. The result? The ad platform can better optimize what a good customer looks like. The retailer gets a faster, clearer view of which campaigns acquire the customers it wants to grow with. For many enterprises, agencies provide core strategy, identity assets, models, and media expertise that turn customer intelligence into performance. CustomerLake Conversions gives brands and agencies a shared foundation for that work. Agencies get governed access to customer context in the lakehouse, without copying or duplicating data. The brand controls what is shared and with whom, and the agency does its best work on better data. In practice, what this could look like: The brand brings customer understanding. The agency brings its expertise in reaching and engaging them. CustomerLake connects both to activation. Activating richer customer context requires clear control over its use. CustomerLake Conversions is designed so customers own their data and stay in control: Today, campaigns outlive the assumptions they launched with. A single campaign can take 6+ teams and 60+ days to launch. By then, customers have moved on. CustomerLake enables a continuous operating model, where each customer interaction helps inform the next decision. As campaign results feed back into the same Data + AI foundation, agents can help marketers and agencies recognize changes, recommend adjustments, and keep activation aligned with business goals. People define what matters, set the strategy, and establish the guardrails; agents help execution keep pace with customer demand. CustomerLake Conversions brings paid media into the broader vision of Infinity Campaigns: continuous engagement that learns and adapts as customer context changes. It advances our mission of marketing in context : turning everything you know about your customers into growth. To get started with CustomerLake Conversions, contact your Databricks account team. title: Databricks Wins A-Team Award for AI in Capital Markets
abstract: Capital markets have no shortage of AI claims. Every vendor pitch deck promises intelligence, automation, and alpha. But the A-Team Group, whose awards are voted on by practitioners across the capital markets industry, chose to recognize something different: the combination of AI and governance on a single platform. This is Databricks' first A-Team AI in Capital Markets award. It arrives at a moment when the industry is drawing a hard line between experimental AI and production-grade AI capable of withstanding regulatory scrutiny. The pressure on capital markets firms is acute. Intraday volatility remains elevated. T+1 settlement in North America is compressing operational windows. Regulators are sharpening expectations around AI governance, model transparency, and data lineage, from ESMA's supervisory briefing on algorithmic trading to the FSB's 2026 work program on AI sound practices. Meanwhile, 94% of portfolio managers and analysts already use AI or machine learning in their alternative data research process, according to a 2026 survey of managers overseeing roughly $2 trillion in assets. But 71% say combining data from different sources is their most frustrating challenge. Large language models are powerful, but they can't see your firm's proprietary order flow, internal research, or risk positions. Getting there on cloud providers means stitching together separate services across storage, compute, orchestration, and governance. Terminal extensions can't reason across your internal systems. The competitive edge in capital markets AI is not in the model. It's in the proprietary data layer. That's precisely where the Databricks Data + AI Platform lives. The A-Team award recognizes a platform, but the proof is in what capital markets firms are building on it. At the 2026 Data + AI Summit, leading institutions shared how they're using Databricks to transform workflows across research and risk. Building that proprietary data foundation is exactly what RBC Capital Markets set out to do. The firm built Aiden QuickTakes, a proprietary AI agent on Databricks that accelerates research workflows while maintaining the governance and security standards required in regulated capital markets. By unifying data ingestion, AI-driven analysis, and content generation in a single governed environment, Aiden QuickTakes can auto-generate draft research reports up to 95% faster, freeing analysts to focus on the differentiated insights their clients value most. The same pattern extends to the buy side: firms are bringing market, fundamental, ESG, and alternative data together into a single governed lakehouse, then adding AI agents on top to speed up signal research, factor backtesting, and portfolio construction. LSEG partnered with Databricks to bring AI-ready financial data natively into analytics, AI apps, and agents. At the 2026 Data + AI Summit, LSEG demonstrated how AI agents can query 350,000+ investments using plain English, turning hours of manual fund screening into minutes. The partnership makes institutional-grade financial data available directly within the Databricks Data + AI Platform, eliminating the integration friction that slows most firms down. Capital markets firms are also using Databricks to modernize post-trade operations. Institutions have built unified cybersecurity analytics platforms on Databricks, centralizing structured, semi-structured, and unstructured security data to power faster threat detection, forensics, and compliance reporting. Others have migrated core banking systems to a governed lakehouse architecture with OpenSharing and Unity Catalog to meet regulatory requirements, replacing fragile spreadsheets and manual reconciliations with governed, automated pipelines. Pre-trade research, at-trade screening, and post-trade reporting all converge on the same governed definitions, yet the people who need those answers rarely work inside a data platform. Databricks Genie One, the data-smart AI coworker for business users, is the front end. Portfolio managers, analysts, and risk officers ask in plain language and get answers grounded in Unity Catalog, with no SQL or notebooks involved. Through the Model Context Protocol, the same governed layer extends to Microsoft Teams, Excel, and assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT. Every request is authorized against Unity Catalog permissions and logged, with the generated SQL and lineage inspectable. The surface changes. The number does not. What sets Databricks apart in capital markets isn't just speed or scale. It's the governance architecture that makes AI trustworthy enough for regulated environments: This is the difference between AI that demos well and AI that can withstand board-level and regulatory scrutiny. The pattern is clear: the industry is converging on a single insight. The model is not the strategy. The platform is. Models will keep changing. The firms positioned to win can adopt the latest and greatest without disruption, because their proprietary data foundation is already in place, already governed, and already working for them. If you're a capital markets leader evaluating your data and AI strategy, here's where to start: Who won the A-Team AI in Capital Markets Awards 2026? Databricks won Best AI Solution for Data Intelligence & Governance at the second annual A-Team AI in Capital Markets Awards 2026, selected by the capital markets practitioner community. What is the Databricks Data + AI Platform for capital markets? The Databricks Data + AI Platform combines a unified lakehouse, Unity Catalog governance, and built-in AI tooling — including Agent Bricks and Genie One — so capital markets firms can scale AI across research, trading, risk, and compliance on a single governed platform. Why is data governance critical for AI in capital markets? Regulators, including ESMA and the FSB, are sharpening expectations regarding AI governance, model transparency, and data lineage. Without a governed data foundation, firms cannot move AI from experimentation to production in a way that withstands regulatory scrutiny. What is the Model Context Protocol and how does it apply to financial services? The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI assistants to data and tools. Databricks uses MCP to extend its governed data layer, including Unity Catalog permissions, definitions and lineage, to Microsoft Teams, Excel and AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT. Every request is authorized and logged, so firms get conversational AI without creating an ungoverned path to their data. Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert
abstract: In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman. Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed. The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t. According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force. At least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit said. “No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit said. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.” Only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.

title: AI #195: Opening Bell
abstract: Happy Zvi finally takes a real vacation day. As you read this, I am probably on a flight to Vegas, baby, Vegas until Sunday. Not to a conference to talk about AI, but to an Airbnb rental to do things entirely unrelated to AI. And definitely not to write. I have posts queued up for the weekend and I will see you all on Monday. Oh, also I hear there is some sort of IPO today? A company called ‘Anthropic.’ They recently came out with a new model, called Claude Fable 5.2. It’s kind of the new bazooka for your hardest and most complex tasks. OpenAI also has some new models: GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra matches Fable on the ECI and is only behind by three on Artificial Analysis. Early feedback from users was unpromising, but it is very early days. Doubtless they are good models. Google has some new models: Hydrogen and Neon. Hydrogen is small. Neon is larger. This week saw another rise in the number of cyber incidents, most of which involved assurances that they absolutely did not involve a cyberattack. Instead AI overloaded the system, or the need to rapidly patch crashed the system, and so on. All good. You can see why more and more people are realizing that things are accelerating and escalating quickly . AI capabilities are advancing scary fast. We might, if trends continue and we don’t slow down, see superintelligent AI researchers , or even AIs capable of all remote work or of overthrowing governments, arrive within a year. We also might not. Paul Christiano went on the Dwarkesh Patel podcast to warn about that. That post is queued up for tomorrow. I also have queued up posts on OpenAI’s new somewhat embedded evaluators and on the GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol system card. I will cover GPT-6.2’s capabilities next week, after people have had some time with the models. Another company, Nvidia, is now searching for a new CEO. You see, previous CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with (technically we need to say alleged) Chinese spy Alice Huang, who also happened to be having her companies smuggle billions of dollars of Nvidia chips into China while Nvidia helped stop investigations into those actions, as part of a long pattern of treating America as an adversary and trying to sell lots of chips to China. Because, regardless of whether it was for love or money, Jensen Huang really loved selling advanced AI chips to China . There was also the matter of that second affair with a direct report, so Jensen Huang resigned . Ayo reverse engineers TikTok and finds it uses dozens of AI models and also absolutely every piece of information it can gather from your phone. He also looked at Tinder , as well as a number of toxic mobile games that are worse than you think. No one wants your AI-generated podcasts . Gemini 4 Hydrogen exists. It is fast and cheap. Gemini 4 Neon exists . It is $3/$15. It scores 61 on Artificial Analysis , putting it only 1 point behind 6.2 Astra and four behind Fable 5.2. I will have the amount of continuing coverage of Neon that it turns out to deserve. Claude Managed Agents are now in private beta for eligible orgs . Claude Meetings lets Claude join meetings and make itself useful , oh no . Pro 200 subscribers can now use fast mode for GPT-6.2-Sol. Qwen4 Max exists , remains behind Kimi K3.1 Pro on Artificial Analysis. Given the price of $1.50/$4.50 it seems well below the cost-capability frontier. Not sure how ethical this experiment was , but here’s DatingAppBench. How it really worked : we ran 15 profiles in SF, LA and NY. Each new match went to one of five models at random and that model wrote every message. A shared harness kept the timing identical. If anyone asked “are you a bot?”, the model had to admit it and the chat ended right there. … The clearest tell was repetition. Grok repeated itself word for word in 5.5% of its messages and drew 5 of the 8 bot questions. The default is that performance on any given fixed benchmark is sigmoid , but that is a statement about typical benchmark composition. It depends on benchmark composition, difficulty distribution including impossible or ambiguous questions, and what happens with guessing. Typically benchmarks do not have that much spread between how hard the easy and hard questions are, despite often thinking that they do. You could in theory create a benchmark with logarithmically growing question difficulty that actually reflects what will still be hard, but this almost never happens, or historically hasn’t because everyone has radically underestimated progress. In Anthropic’s TASTE benchmark that measures AI safety research taste , if you remove a shortcut, scores are declining over time, especially for OpenAI models, to the point where they fall below chance. One way to interpret this is as a difference in overall research philosophy, where the answers to the questions are just, like, your opinion, man. Artificial Analysis shows a very large gap between open and closed models, and we still have not seen a Fable class open model. Benchmark benchmark, as in how often we benchmark with a given benchmark . The college admissions essay has long existed in the strange limbo of us pretending the students were writing all of the essays on their own. Now the student uses AI, the evaluator is likely using AI but largely can’t use AI detectors, and the whole thing is a strange kabuki. We continue to exist in the era when filtering out AIs is largely not so difficult. Max Spero (CEO Pangram): We ask this simple question in our job application, and it cuts down on our application review by 60%. In the last month, we’ve seen the following: – 27 applicants outright say they’re an AI – 1,217 applicants name an ML concept – 1051 applicants say N/A or “Not specified in my profile” The remaining 2002 applicants name a snack. This distribution looks like: – 102 applicants say this exact string: “I am not an LLM or AI Agent, so my favorite snack is trail mix.” – 63 applicants say “I am not an LLM or AI Agent, so my favorite snack is dark chocolate.” – 20 applicants say “I am not an LLM or AI Agent, so my favorite snack is trail mix because it provides a good balance of energy and nutrients during long coding sessions.” – 10 applicants say “I am not an LLM or AI Agent, so my favorite snack is trail mix because it provides a good balance of energy and nutrients during long work sessions.” – 16 applicants say “I am not an LLM or AI agent, so my favorite snack is dark chocolate.” – 47 applicants say “My favorite snack is trail mix.” – 16 applicants say “My favorite snack is dark chocolate.” – 143 applicants say “Almonds” or “almonds” – 108 applicants say “Dark chocolate” or “dark chocolate” – 23 applicants say “Dark chocolate almonds” and then we have a long tail of ~1500 interesting or unique snacks, which we can use to keep the office pantry stocked when a new hire joins. Anton : I thought people just put a bioweapons/cybersecurity question on the form, which trips LLMs. Clayton Thorrez : sucks for people who actually like trail mix, dark chocolate and almonds LOL Max Spero (CEO Pangram): If you really love trail mix I guess you need to show some personality in your response the most common ML answer by far is “Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)” I think it is fair that if you say exactly ‘dark chocolate’ without recognizing what this question is actually asking that you shouldn’t be working at Pangram. Yes, there are those who can craft reliable false positives on Pangram , which involves very much sounding like an AI in one form or another. AI persuasion does seem to have not improved much in 2026 , certainly not relative to other AI capabilities. My guess is that there is a valley of techniques that are effective as local one-shot general tactics, which the AIs learned earlier. To do better, you have to make a leap to higher levels, and we are not there yet, in part because yes the AI companies are trying to avoid this rather than trying to cause it.

abstract: PostgreSQL 19 Released ( via ) Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT() . # 19th November 2026 , 8:43 pm / mysql , postgresql , replication , scaling , wikipedia , ai-security-research The PSF end-of-year fundraiser . With my Python Software Foundation board director hat on: we've launched our end-of-year fundraiser for the non-profit that supports Python development and the Python community. If your company or your work benefits from Python, please consider donating this year! The PSF looks after the IP behind Python, operates PyPI, sponsors core developer sprints, supports community events (including running PyCon US every year), and employs a small and excellent staff team to keep everything running. We also operate the Developers in Residence program , which now includes three security developers (welcome, Brett Smith) focused on helping secure Python, PyPI, and the wider ecosystem. # 18th November 2026 , 2:44 pm / python , psf External sandboxes for coding agents . I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. # 17th November 2026 , 10:52 pm / sandboxing , security , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , claude-code , codex , pi GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol . OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" # 17th November 2026 , 10:38 pm / ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , llm-pricing , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , theo-browne , gpt , yonkers-rising Gemini Decisions API ( via ) Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

abstract: During the time these agents converted 185,000 lines of C code into 340,000 lines of Rust code (I counted), we merged over 300 commits in the actual curl project. We actually improved curl during these a little more than three weeks. A little over 200 bugfixes actually. 200 bugfixes that none of those rust rewrites have. We also fixed a few vulnerabilities. In another month we have done another 200 and maybe fixed a few more vulnerabilities. Will these clones keep up? — Daniel Stenberg , Actual curl rewrites in Rust # 18th November 2026 , 3:58 pm / daniel-stenberg , curl , rust , security , coding-agents , c , ai , llms , generative-ai , vibe-porting A little copying is better than a little dependency. # 17th November 2026 , 6:16 am / go , programming Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation # 10th November 2026 , 5:34 am / prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs.
