title: AI will not make you rich (2025)
abstract:
Read on: Kindle How to read on Kindle 1. Download the EPUB Select Kindle to download this article as an EPUB. 2. Send it to your Kindle Open Send to Kindle , sign in to your Amazon account, and upload the EPUB file. Send the file, then sync your Kindle or Kindle app to find it in your library. Click here to subscribe to print for your office or home. Fortunes are made by entrepreneurs and investors when revolutionary technologies enable waves of innovative, investable companies. Think of the railroad, the Bessemer process, electric power, the internal combustion engine, or the microprocessor—each of which, like a stray spark in a fireworks factory, set off decades of follow-on innovations, permeated every part of society, and catapulted a new set of inventors and investors into power, influence, and wealth. Yet some technological innovations, though societally transformative, generate little in the way of new wealth; instead, they reinforce the status quo. Fifteen years before the microprocessor, another revolutionary idea, shipping containerization, arrived at a less propitious time, when technological advancement was a Red Queen’s race, and inventors and investors were left no better off for non-stop running. Anyone who invests in the new new thing must answer two questions: First, how much value will this innovation create? And second, who will capture it? Information and communication technology (ICT) was a revolution whose value was captured by startups and led to thousands of newly rich founders, employees, and investors. In contrast, shipping containerization was a revolution whose value was spread so thin that in the end, it made only a single founder temporarily rich and only a single investor a little bit richer. Is generative AI more like the former or the latter? Will it be the basis of many future industrial fortunes, or a net loser for the investment community as a whole, with a few zero-sum winners here and there? There are ways to make money investing in the fruits of AI, but they will depend on assuming the latter—that it is once again a less propitious time for inventors and investors, that AI model builders and application companies will eventually compete each other into an oligopoly, and that the gains from AI will accrue not to its builders but to customers. A lot of the money pouring into AI is therefore being invested in the wrong places, and aside from a couple of lucky early investors, those who make money will be the ones with the foresight to get out early. The microprocessor was revolutionary , but the people who invented it at Intel in 1971 did not see it that way—they just wanted to avoid designing desktop calculator chipsets from scratch every time. But outsiders realized they could use the microprocessor to build their own personal computers, and enthusiasts did. Thousands of tinkerers found configurations and uses that Intel never dreamed of. This distributed and permissionless invention kicked off a “great surge of development,” as the economist Carlota Perez calls it, triggered by technology but driven by economic and societal forces. [1] There was no real demand for personal computers in the early 1970s; they were expensive toys. But the experimenters laid the technical groundwork and built a community. Then, around 1975, a step-change in the cost of microprocessors made the personal computer market viable. The Intel 8080 had an initial list price of $360 ($2,300 in today’s dollars). MITS could barely turn a profit on its Altair at a bulk price of $75 each ($490 today). But when MOS Technologies started selling its 6502 for $25 ($150 today), Steve Wozniak could afford to build a prototype Apple. The 6502 and the similarly priced Zilog Z80 forced Intel’s prices down. The nascent PC community started spawning entrepreneurs and a score of companies appeared, each with a slightly different product. You couldn’t have known in the mid-1970s that the PC (and PC-like products, such as ATMs, POS terminals, smartphones, etc.) would revolutionize everything. While Steve Jobs was telling investors that every household would someday have a personal computer (a wild underestimate, as it turned out), others questioned the need for personal computers at all. As late as 1979, Apple’s ads didn’t tell you what a personal computer could do—it asked what you did with it. [2] The established computer manufacturers (IBM, HP, DEC) had no interest in a product their customers weren’t asking for. Nobody “needed” a computer, and so PCs weren’t bought—they were sold. Flashy startups like Apple and Sinclair used hype to get noticed, while companies with footholds in consumer electronics like Atari, Commodore, and Tandy/RadioShack used strong retail connections to put their PCs in front of potential customers. The market grew slowly at first, accelerating only as experiments led to practical applications like the spreadsheet, introduced in 1979. As use grew, observation of use caused a reduction in uncertainty, leading to more adoption in a self-reinforcing cycle. This kind of gathering momentum takes time in every technological wave: It took almost 30 years for electricity to reach half of American households, for example, and it took about the same amount of time for personal computers. [3] When a technological revolution changes everything, it takes a huge amount of innovation, investment, storytelling, time, and plain old work. It also sucks up all the money and talent available. Like Kuhn’s paradigms in science, any technology not part of the wave’s techno-economic paradigm will seem like a sideshow. [4] Source : [3] The nascent growth of PCs attracted investors—venture capitalists—who started making risky bets on new companies. This development incentivized more inventors, entrepreneurs, and researchers, which in turn drew in more speculative capital. Companies like IBM, the computing behemoth before the PC, saw poor relative performance. They didn’t believe the PC could survive long enough to become capable in their market and didn’t care about new, small markets that wanted a cheaper solution. Retroactively, we give the PC pioneers the powers of prophets rather than visionaries. But at the time, nobody outside of a small group of early adopters paid any attention. Establishment media like The New York Times didn’t take the PC seriously until after IBM’s was introduced in August 1981. In the entire year of 1976, when Apple Computer was founded, the NYT mentioned PCs only four times. [5] Apparently, only the crazy ones, the misfits, the rebels, and the troublemakers were paying attention. Source : [5] It’s the element of surprise that should strike us most forcefully when we compare the early days of the computer revolution to today. No one took note of personal computers in the 1970s. In 2025, AI is all we seem to talk about. Big companies hate surprises. That’s why uncertainty makes a perfect moat for startups. Apple would never have survived IBM entering the market in 1979, and only lived to compete another day after raising $100 million in its 1980 IPO. It was the only remaining competitor after the IBM-induced winnowing. [6] Source : [6] As the tech took hold and started to show promise, innovations in software, memory, and peripherals like floppy disk drives and modems joined it. They reinforced one another, with each advance putting pressure on the technologies adjacent to it. When any part of the system held back the other parts, investors rushed to fund that sector. As increases in PC memory allowed more complicated software, for example, there became a need for more external storage, which caused VC Dave Marquardt to invest in disk drive manufacturer Seagate in 1980. Seagate gave Marquardt a 40x return when it went public in 1981. Other investors noticed, and some $270 million was plowed into the industry in the following three years.

title: The AI Superintelligence Debate Has Serious Flaws
abstract:
Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen Yet trying for it may still be disastrous 12 min read McKibillo Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied , “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN , “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.” These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks. These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia. Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology. I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm. Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper , statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians , a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity). Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028. But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3 , to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4 , however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns . This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs. Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics , which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized , “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation. McKibillo The Game of Superintelligence How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead Key • Idea: A concept, argument, or vision • Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development • Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress 1. Alan Turing 1936 Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI. REALITY CHECK Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm. 2. I. J. Good 1965 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” 3. Backpropagation 1986 Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks. 4. Vernor Vinge 1993 Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.” REALITY CHECK Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A ­faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess. 5. Nick Bostrom & Eliezer Yudkowsky 1990s–2000s Bostrom and Yudkowsky discuss superintelligence in Extropian circles, then spread the idea to effective-­altruist and rationalist circles, respectively. 6. Deep learning breakthroughs 2010s Larger models, more data, and greater computing power produce rapid ­improvements in AI capabilities. 7. The race to self-improving AI 2020s Dario Amodei and other AI leaders set their sights on superintelligence, with recursive self-improvement proposed as a path toward it. 8. Reality check 2020s François Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain. YOU ARE HERE 2026 AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion? THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES 1.

title: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
abstract:
Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime ( https://maritime.sh ). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents. Demo:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY  There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is: You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins. It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem. We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction: 1. Agent lifecycle management. There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime.
There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up. 2. Custom environments. Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies.
Some agents need access to private networks to interact with customer-specific things on prem, or residential IPs, or the ability to restrict network access completely. 3. Cost optimization. If you’re selling a personal assistant for $20/month, a sandbox that costs $0.04/hour comes out to roughly $29/month if you keep it running continuously, not including LLM inference, storage, etc. There is a way to combat this though, which is to optimize sandbox usage with auto-snapshotting, making things event-driven, mounting S3 buckets to agent environments via FUSE for cheap storage, cold-tiering snapshots, etc. All roads lead to… building more infrastructure. So what did we build differently? We give each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. On top of the compute, we built a lot of composable services: provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking, login handoffs, all the things you’d need for production agents. We also spent a huge amount of time optimizing cost. A lot of thought was put into things such as scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots, hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering, and other optimizations while balancing these with performance metrics like latency. As a result, Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month (unlimited usage for that $1), with additional resources available as needed. Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure. Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab. We started Maritime together this March because of all the issues we faced with trying to deploy agents to the cloud during our research. We want your feedback. If you're building an agent product, what did you have to build on top of sandboxes to make them work? We want to know about all the workarounds and weird things you’ve had to build. Are there things you’ve tried to build with VMs but couldn’t? Does Maritime fit your needs? Is there a feature we’re missing that would make us more enticing? Happy to answer any questions in the comments.  https://maritime.sh

title: LLM assisted reverse engineering
abstract:
I have been hacking both hardware and software for 2 decades. Previously manually. But in 2026 with the help of AIs the proccess is greatly sped up. Below I will describe my proccess briefly or how I do it. Set Up Tools which I mostly use are these: TOOL use DeepSeek Harness + Deepseek v4.1 Flash Thats the AI I am using. Occasionaly I use Codex with Luna or Terra but Deepseek is super performant, fast and cheap Ghidra + MCP bridge The best in the market, free, disassembler and decompiler. With the MCP bridge agents can use it very well radare2 and kuna CLI disassemblers and decompilers. Not as good as Ghidra but much faster and possibly better usable for AIs Process What I basically do nowadays is just point the agent at the binary to be analysed and use my set of dedicated agent skills. Rest usually takes care of itself. But putting the skills besides, the flow is basically this. Find binary type, platform, build etc - based on this using appropriate decompiler (note - current AIs do fairly well with just disassembly . ie pure x86 or ARM instructions). Command agent to document all findings along the way to MD files. This serves several purposes. They become notes for your own understanding. They help the agent not lose the track after compaction / handoff to different agent. And last but not least, it helps the agent work more effectively, not get lost in circles etc. More about this later. Ask the agent to analyse basic structure. Main functions, main branching, imported functions etc of given binary. By binary I mean whatever. Desktop executable, website or firmware image. Once I have this basic overview I can usually proceed any way I need to do modifications to the original binary or build mods or just help me understand it better. On some occasions some things are not easily resolvable by simple disassembly or decompilation. In those cases you can do: Let the agent debug given binary and set breakpoints on specific parts to help it figure out given inner workings. Use logging. Either by somehow enabling it in the original binary or by making a probe (and this can mean many things) that injects to the original binary and records you via logs (to file) whatever is needed to resolve given feature. Give agent outside access - ie computer use for desktop apps, or api controllable emulator for running and controlling given firmware. Ask agent to try different approach. But you must be specific. Ie when it gets stuck in disasembly by following xrefs, ask it to try to follow strings in the binary instead. Read the entire LLM conversation and thinking. Current LLMs are smart but they still sometimes get to a narrow approach. By reading the traces you can often instinctively figure the agent it going into a blind path and give it suggestion as to how it might be approached better. That however skill of your own to have. SKILLS Here are some of my major skills I use frequently. Matt Pottock - Grill me It gives you several questions when your input might be valuable. I usually use it with this prompt: text Use skill /grill-me to ask me up to 5 questions
whose answers are crucial for your further progress.
Ask only one question at a time. mattpocock / skills Shell Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab. Ghidra / other RE tooling skill It helps a ton to have a skill where your specific reverse engineering tooling is described. Ie to use radare2 or kuna. Or description of how to use the MCP Ghidra bridge and for what. Without such a skill, agents often give up too quickly getting lost, not knowing how to do the actual disassembly / decompilation. ioma8 / ghidra-decompile-skill Java Agent skill + 22 Ghidra scripts for fast targeted decompilation, and the fix for GhidraMCP extension/Ghidra version mismatches. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab. Hypothesis debugging That is also my own skill. Its related to how I wrote earlier how important it is to make the agent document everything into MD files. This skill forces agent who is getting stuck to follow this loop: Make a hypothesis of why / how something works. Write it down into CSV table of hypotheses, saved on disc. Design experiment (probe, logging, ...) which will definitively prove or disprove this hypothesis. Record the result. Repeat. This is variation of scientific method and it significantly helps agents when they are getting stuck on some problem. Stops it going in circles. By forcing it to do definitive experiments. No endless guessing and trying random things. This one is crucial in my opinion. I made it public too, so other can benefit from it. ioma8 / hypothesis-debugging Agent skill for hypothesis-driven debugging — one testable hypothesis at a time, logged and validated in a CSV loop. Open repo ↗ Opens in a new tab. Implementation of hacks and probes For implementing anything I basically go for 2 toolings. Python but with UV tooling. UV tooling allows to make custom envs super quickly and portably. Also allows to make single-file, inline dependencies scripts. Python is great for prototyping or quickly making probes or even decompilation helpers. Rust for actual implementation of given hack. Whenever it is possible I am using rust for this. It has many reasons but he two main are: it is very elegant language for me personally to work with and it provides brutally good feedback loops to the agent when it iterates - the compiler is very strict and points the agent immediately to any possible memory or syntax issues he might be heading to. Of course rust has also its downsides, like slower compile times, but overal its mature language with plethora of build targets (I have implemented in it webs, desktop apps, hacks / trainers but even firmwares for various embedded languages). My hacking successes With the AI assisted reverse engineering I was able to achieve such crazy reverse engineering succeses, in the last 6 months, which would take me years each on its own, if done by hands. Reverse engineered and hacked Alphasmart NEO typewriting device Completely mapped communication protocols of many devices like EmWave biofeedback device or both my Sony Alpha mirrorless cameras. Allowing me to make custom desktop and mobile apps for file transfer, wireless control and more. I even managed to make this way a wireless webcam from my A7III mirrorless camera. Hacked into and developed custom firmwares for musical synthesizers: Arturia MiniFreak Teenage Engineering OP-Z Akai MPC Sample Made custom firmware for Xteink X4 ebook reader Fixed driver for old HP printer for MacOs Cracked tons of license-locked abandonware softwares from my youth Developed custom lightweight Evernote client And many more Sometimes its a thin boundary between reverse engineering and software development. Sometimes you just decipher the proprietary save file format of the ugly paid app and then move into the clean software development phase of building your new, totally unique editor, to work with these files. (yes I made custom Photoshop too and its not the ArtCraft suite - I did it about a year before them, just for me). Final thoughts Reverse engineering and hacking into old softwares or devices has always been a hobby for me. I understand assembly, I understand hardware. But it was long and tedious process. With the cheap accesibility to smart LLM tools in these days, this hobby took dramatic turn for me. I do not miss manually analyzing the assembly instructions. But I love quickly getting the results. Yes my long experience helps me steer the agents the correct way. But that is also fun. And I am learning a ton of things along the way. I wish everyone would try to do some hacks of his own. For me the hobby is driven by curiosity. And LLMs didn't take that away. They gave me turbo boost to my wonderings and explorations. Let's free our minds! Edit: We are getting popular on HN! Didnt expect this one day after deploying my blog! Super happy!

title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
abstract: Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi. Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN:  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073 . It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races. Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself. At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans. There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack. Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc). When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI. We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead. You can get started with `npm create factory`. It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!  https://factory.mastra.ai   https://github.com/mastra-ai/template-factory

title: Ruby2ßhell: Pre-authentication RCE on stock Rails
abstract:
Affected software Ruby versions Ruby series Affected Fixed in 4.0 4.0.0 to 4.0.9 4.0.10 3.4 3.4.0 to 3.4.12 3.4.13 3.3 3.3.0 to 3.3.13 3.3.14 3.2 and older All releases back to 2.4.0 EOL Frameworks The bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration . Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable. Framework Status on an affected Ruby Rails Affected Sinatra (classic style) Affected Other frameworks and plain Rack Not exposed by default Self-hosted software These products bundle their own Ruby, so the fix has to come from the vendor. Products marked Vulnerable have no fixed release yet: every current version is vulnerable. Software Affected versions Fixed in Status GitLab 19.6.0 and earlier None Vulnerable GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 and earlier None Vulnerable Chatwoot 4.20.0 and earlier None Vulnerable Mastodon 4.7.5 and earlier 4.7.6 , 4.6.12 , 4.5.22 , 4.4.29 Patched OpenProject 17.9.7 and earlier 17.9.8 , 17.8.3 Patched Discourse base image Before 2.0.20261119-0203 2.0.20261119-0203 Patched Updated 19 November 2026 at 23:30 UTC . Remediation Your deployment Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14 , 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 . Self-hosted software Install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products. Technical details Root cause Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital ß . Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS , but the loop only bounds-checks one ( to < to_end ). 1 while ( * pp < end && to < to_end) { /* room for one byte */ 2 code = * ( * pp) ++ ; 3 if (code == SHARP_s) { 4 if (flags & ONIGENC_CASE_UPCASE) { 5 * to ++ = 'S' ; /* first byte */ 6 code = 'S' ; 7 } 8 /* ... */ 9 } 10 /* ... */ 11 * to ++ = code; /* second byte, unchecked */ 12 } The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each ß adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte. The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase , swapcase , downcase(:fold) and casecmp? . UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected. Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f . Primitive A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S ( 0x53 ) when upcasing or s ( 0x73 ) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length. Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds. Proof of concept We'll be publishing a proof of concept demonstrating remote code execution on stock Rails on 25 November 2026 , or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix by then. Credits Veria Labs found this vulnerability independently and was the first to demonstrate remote code execution. The Ruby security advisory also credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic with reporting the underlying primitive. Additional discoverers include Moritz Sanft in collaboration with OpenAI.

title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion
abstract:
Security advisories: multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion Posted by mame on 18 Nov 2026 Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading. CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5 : Heap buffer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x : Double free in regular expression compilation Ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px : Integer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive regular expression matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way. GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w : Heap buffer overflow in regular expression compilation Ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4 : Heap buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s Ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s . Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h : Out-of-bounds read in case-insensitive backreference matching Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process. Affected versions Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12 Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9 Recommended action We strongly recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14. Ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached their end of life and will not receive these fixes. title: Do not buy RAM, compress
abstract:
Do not buy RAM, compress! 19 Nov, 2026 AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations.
Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option.
Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in zram , a solution to compress memory. Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it.
Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM.
Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default.
Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines.
Most other distributions do not have it enabled. Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes.
What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4. I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app.
Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression.
This could have cut our Cloud spend in half! How it looks in practice I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. title: DaisyRose-27B
abstract:
All posts Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. We are releasing BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget. DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above 1 . The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes. High-quality Training Data We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 of them made it into the final training set. The training tasks are selected based on three criteria. Each task targets a mistake the original model makes. We ran the original Qwen3.8-27B on every training task and carefully redesigned each one so that it brings out the mistakes we want the model to stop making. We then tuned each task until its solve rate fell within a suitable range, neither too easy nor too hard for the model to learn from. Every task is a long job with several problems chained together. Each task entails a chain of interdependent problems, so an agent has to navigate through multiple stages of reasoning, planning, and execution. Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in the sandbox, with more than 100 tool-calls and more than 256k output tokens. There is no room for reward hacking. We reviewed every task along with the model's attempts at it. Any task that could be passed without really solving it, or that had a design flaw, was fixed or removed before training. Efficient training backend RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization. 57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash. 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs. Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady. Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs. Robust sandbox service During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time. Reliable as it grew. The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory. 80% lower cost. Our cloud infrastructure cost for the project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes. Try DaisyRose-27B, or train your own You can download DaisyRose-27B from Hugging Face , and you can train your own agents with our open source reinforcement learning framework Miles . DaisyRose-27B is one example of what high-quality data and efficient infrastructure can make possible. We are bringing this approach to teams building specialized models, with a focus on improving the capabilities they need while preserving the model’s broader strengths. If you are exploring post-training for your own model, reach out at contact@radixark.ai . We are deeply grateful to Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and to the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B, the foundation of our work. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, as well as other open-source projects, including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor. How we evaluated: Terminal Bench 4.1 is averaged over 8 runs per task, using our internal mini-swe-agent harness with summarization turned on. Terminal Bench 2.1 is averaged over 5 runs per task, using the Terminus 2 harness. DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE Bench Pro v2 are averaged over 8 and 5 runs per task, both using the mini-swe-agent harness. HLE (text-only) is averaged over 5 runs per problem, graded by GPT-6 Luna, with no tools. IFBench is averaged over 4 runs on each of its 300 prompts, scored by the official allenai/IFBench scorer as prompt-level loose accuracy on the final response, with the thinking left out. GPQA Diamond is averaged over 8 runs on each of its 198 questions, using the simple-evals multiple-choice template and answer extraction, with the answer order reshuffled on every run. ↩

title: Making 8-page foldable zines from a single A4 sheet in the browser
abstract:
Paper, folds, and what’s new in fanzines.app 19 Nov, 2026 A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work. If you've never made one, the fold is simple. Take a single A4 sheet of paper, fold it in half three times, open it back up, and cut along the center crease with scissors. Fold the sheet into a cross and close it, and you have an 8-page booklet with no staples or glue. I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes. Why fanzines.app exists The part I never liked was laying out the flat sheet on the computer before printing. Because the A4 paper folds back on itself, the pages sit in a strange order and the top row has to be upside down: ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
│ 6 │ 5 │ 4 │ 3 │ ← upside down (180°)
├─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤
│ Back │ Cover │ 1 │ 2 │ ← right-side up
└─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘ I got tired of rotating pictures and double-checking columns in Photoshop every time I wanted to print a new zine, so I built fanzines.app . In the browser, you lay out each page right-side up with photos and text. When you export, the app places all 8 panels onto the A4 grid with the top row rotated 180 degrees and generates a 300 DPI PDF. Everything stays local in the browser; no photos are uploaded to a server. Over the last few days, I rebuilt the editor around the things that kept getting in my way when I sat down to make a zine. Fixing how pages are paired In the first version, the sidebar listed the 8 pages in a plain two-column grid. It paired the Front Cover with Page 1, Page 2 with Page 3, Page 4 with Page 5, and Page 6 with the Back Cover. It looked tidy on screen, but it didn't match the physical booklet. When you hold a folded zine, the front cover sits alone on the right. Open it and Page 1 faces Page 2 across the fold, then 3 faces 4, 5 faces 6, and the back cover ends up alone on the left. The sidebar now groups the page thumbnails into those real spreads, in reading order. I also added a Spread view on the canvas. While you're editing Page 1, Page 2 sits beside it at lower opacity so you can check how the two facing pages sit together before printing. Clicking the dimmed page switches straight to editing it. Smaller changes that make the editor less fussy When I make a photo zine, I usually start with a folder of 8 photos already picked out. Now you can drag the whole batch onto the editor window, and the sidebar highlights which pages will take each photo in reading order before you drop them. I changed the side panel too. Early on, clicking a photo opened four coordinate inputs ( X , Y , Width , Height ). I rarely needed to type coordinates; mostly I wanted a photo to fill the page, fit inside the margins, or sit centered. Fill, Fit, and Center now sit at the top of the inspector and in a small toolbar above the selection. The exact fields are still in a collapsible section at the bottom, now in millimeters (for the 74.25 × 105 mm folded panel) and points for text. Before downloading the PDF, a Review step shows the full unfolded A4 sheet with toggles for cut/fold lines and a 5 mm safe margin. Most home printers clip a few millimeters around the edge of an A4 sheet, so the safe margin scales the layout to about 95% to keep the covers intact. A couple of other additions: the editor now works on phone screens (one page at a time with a thumbnail strip along the bottom), and the site is available in English as well as Spanish . Changing the language keeps your current pages. Thanks for reading, Wil You can create your own zine in English or Spanish at fanzines.app #tech #zines

title: The Magic of Partial Evaluation
abstract:
There are certain ideas in software that are simply beautiful. It doesn't matter if they have any practical use. It doesn't matter that you will never convince your coworkers to consider them. There is just something captivating about the way some computational systems work. For me, the most beautiful pieces of software are those that reveal something about the nature of programming languages. Programming languages are my obsession. I have never met a problem that couldn't be solved by introducing yet another programming language. Solving a problem at the programming language level is about solving the meta problem. Instead of trying to solve a particular problem, we take a step back and ask how we can solve a whole class of problems at once. So when I find something that makes me rethink the nature of programming languages, I start rethinking computation as a whole. One of these incredibly beautiful but tricky concepts goes by the name partial evaluation. If you are fascinated by interpreters and compilers, partial evaluation will teach you how they are related, and how you can get a compiler for free. Partial Evaluation Easy Mode # Partial evaluation has been a fascination of mine for a while. But this whole thing came up when James Long announced he had revived Meta's partial evaluator for JavaScript called prepack. When I first heard about prepack, I had some high hopes and expectations for the project, but was sadly let down. This revival brought to light those same dreams. But sadly, just as with the original aim, prepack was not designed for beauty, but for practicality. So I figured it was time to renew my own efforts. Yes, in some ways this is a post repping my own library I'm releasing. But I'm not doing this because I want it to be used. I'm doing this because it lets you play with the idea I find so beautiful. That is what this post is about. Doing Partial Evaluation by Hand # Consider the following code: function factorial ( n ) { if ( n <= 1 ) return 1 ; return n * factorial ( n - 1 ) ; } factorial ( 5 ) ; As a person who reads code, you can think about how this code computes and what answer it will give. But you can do more than just give the answer. You can see the expanded form of this particular code for these particular calls. This code is spiritually the same as the following expression, once we expand it out. 5 * ( 4 * ( 3 * ( 2 * 1 ) ) ) In this case, there is really nothing at all that this code needs to do at runtime. A sufficiently smart compiler will just run this code directly at compile time and give the answer. But this is a bit less clear if things come in at runtime. function power ( base , exponent ) { if ( exponent === 0 ) return 1 ; return base * power ( base , exponent - 1 ) ; } power ( process . argv [ 2 ] , 5 ) It might seem like we can't do anything here, but again, if you are used to thinking about how programs run, you can trace this out and realize this is just the same as: process . argv [ 2 ] * ( process . argv [ 2 ] * ( process . argv [ 2 ] * ( process . argv [ 2 ] * ( process . argv [ 2 ] * 1 ) ) ) ) What we have done in both of these cases is called partial evaluation. In the first, it was a trivial case because everything was statically known. But in this latter case, we have reduced a program down into the essentials of its dynamic structure. There are no recursive function calls left. All of this has been expanded as far as it could till we get just the dynamic parts of the code remaining. The Big Idea # This intuitive notion of partial evaluation is all you need to know to appreciate the beauty here. Partial evaluation just evaluates the part of the program we can evaluate at build time and leaves all the rest. When we do this with certain programs in certain combinations, we get some quite surprising, incredible behavior. function calculate ( expr ) { if ( typeof expr === "number" ) return expr ; switch ( expr [ 0 ] ) { case "+" : return calculate ( expr [ 1 ] ) + calculate ( expr [ 2 ] ) ; case "-" : return calculate ( expr [ 1 ] ) - calculate ( expr [ 2 ] ) ; case "*" : return calculate ( expr [ 1 ] ) * calculate ( expr [ 2 ] ) ; case "/" : return calculate ( expr [ 1 ] ) / calculate ( expr [ 2 ] ) ; default : throw new Error ( "Unknown operator" ) ; } } calculate ( [ "+" , 1 , [ "*" , 2 , 3 ] ] ) ; Here we have a very simple interpreter for a language that just supports arithmetic. For the above expression, you should be able to think about how we could start "partially" evaluating it. (In this case, it can be a full evaluation.) If this kind of partial evaluation isn't quite clicking for you, I've put the steps below to hopefully help it make sense. calculate ( [ "+" , 1 , [ "*" , 2 , 3 ] ] ) → calculate ( 1 ) + calculate ( [ "*" , 2 , 3 ] ) → 1 + calculate ( [ "*" , 2 , 3 ] ) → 1 + ( calculate ( 2 ) * calculate ( 3 ) ) → 1 + ( 2 * calculate ( 3 ) ) → 1 + ( 2 * 3 ) → 1 + 6 → 7 This is a simple evaluation of the code. But what happens if we throw a value we don't know into the expression? calculate ( [ "+" , Number ( process . argv [ 2 ] ) , [ "*" , 2 , 3 ] ] ) → calculate ( Number ( process . argv [ 2 ] ) ) + calculate ( [ "*" , 2 , 3 ] ) → Number ( process . argv [ 2 ] ) + calculate ( [ "*" , 2 , 3 ] ) → Number ( process . argv [ 2 ] ) + ( calculate ( 2 ) * calculate ( 3 ) ) → Number ( process . argv [ 2 ] ) + ( 2 * calculate ( 3 ) ) → Number ( process . argv [ 2 ] ) + ( 2 * 3 ) → Number ( process . argv [ 2 ] ) + 6 Here we can see that clear partial evaluation difference. We don't know how to evaluate Number(process.argv[2]) . We have no idea what the answer to that will be. But as part of this process, we do know some partial information about it. For example, when we get to if ( typeof expr === "number" ) return expr ; we know that Number(process.argv[2]) is indeed a number. So we can partially evaluate it further. Hopefully this is all making sense. But if you are like me, this all might seem a bit trivial and uninteresting. So let's look at a more complicated example. function brainfuck ( code , input = "" ) { const tape = new Uint8Array ( 30000 ) ; const jumps = { } , stack = [ ] ; let pointer = 0 , inputPointer = 0 , output = "" ; for ( let i = 0 ; i < code . length ; i ++ ) { if ( code [ i ] === "[" ) stack . push ( i ) ; if ( code [ i ] === "]" ) { const start = stack . pop ( ) ; jumps [ start ] = i ; jumps [ i ] = start ; } } for ( let i = 0 ; i < code . length ; i ++ ) { switch ( code [ i ] ) { case ">" : pointer ++ ; break ; case "<" : pointer -- ; break ; case "+" : tape [ pointer ] ++ ; break ; case "-" : tape [ pointer ] -- ; break ; case "." : output += String . fromCharCode ( tape [ pointer ] ) ; break ; case "," : tape [ pointer ] = inputPointer < input . length ? input . charCodeAt ( inputPointer ++ ) : 0 ; break ; case "[" : if ( ! tape [ pointer ] ) i = jumps [ i ] ; break ; case "]" : if ( tape [ pointer ] ) i = jumps [ i ] ; break ; } } return output ; } brainfuck ( "++++++++++[>+++++++>++++++++++>+++>+<<<<-]>++.>+.+++++++..+++.>++.<<+++++++++++++++.>.+++.------.--------.>+.>." ) ; Here we have a brainfuck interpreter. And the example program we want to partially evaluate does not require any input at all (in brainfuck , is the way you get input). So when we go to partially evaluate this, we will just get an answer. In this case, this program is actually brainfuck's "hello world". But what about a program with input? function main ( ) { return brainfuck ( ",>++[>+++[>++++[<<<+>>>-]<-]<-]<." , process . argv [ 2 ] ) } When we do our partial evaluation, we get the following: function main ( b ) { let a ; a : { a = process . argv [ 2 ] ; a = a === void 0 ? "" : a ; if ( 0 < a . length ) { a = a . charCodeAt ( 0 ) ; break a ; } a = 0 ; } a = ( a & 255 ) + 24 & 255 ; return String . fromCharCode ( a ) ; } What is this? A compiled brainfuck program!

title: Show HN: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you
abstract:
People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here. It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work. The system can also follow theorems and proofs and string together their dependencies, but I haven't made that a focus yet. There's no Lean support, for example. If anyone's interested in that, I'd love to hear it. I want to build this by iterating with the people who use it: a tool that uses AI not to bypass the creative process, but to bring new tools to it. There's a free tier, and if you email hello@foolscap.works I'll send you a code for 50% off. This is my first product, so feedback of any kind is welcome. Thanks,
David

title: OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem
abstract:
October 27, 2026 · kixelated OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem On a previous episode, I flamed OpenAI for using WebRTC and it went viral on Hacker News . thx A huge shoutout to Sean DuBois and Justin Uberti (WebRTC experts at OpenAI) for reaching out after my unhinged rant.
You could have just said @kixelated ur dumb but you didn’t. Alas, my divinely anointed crusade against WebRTC is not over.
deus vult Hot Take Alert Let’s say you’re a vibe coder at a frontier lab working on a voice AI product. Let’s say you’re making (and burning) an obscene amount of cash. Let’s say one of your users vocalizes: what is le capital of France? If your AI ever replies with: I’m sorry, you broke up, can you repeat that? You fucked up .
You picked WebRTC for voice AI. The Danger that Lurks Beneath You boot up your favorite application: ChatGPT™. You click on the microphone and grunt: What is le capital of France? OH NO , hypothetical sudden packet loss .
A kraken nibbles on some underwater cable.
All too common I’m afraid. WebRTC is designed for conference calls, aka real humans and real voices.
It is hyper aggressive and will drop any late audio packets to keep latency real-time .
Just like Leonardo DiCaprio, anything above 30ms is too old. WebRTC gives up on late audio NET What is le capital of France? What is le capital of France? What is le capital of France? What is le capital of France? “France is a country in Western Europe.” ▶ spoken / understood received, not yet understood lost forever What is le France? This kind of sucks for a voice AI product .
You walk out of wifi range, hit a cellular dead zone, or starlink terminal switches satellites.
Oops, your tokens are wasted , or worse, AI tries to guess what you said . WebRTC can usually detect packet loss and retransmit.
But retransmissions are disabled by default for audio.
And even when enabled, the audio jitter buffer won’t wait for them. But why not? Isn’t this networking 101?
Just send that shit again? It’s because of us . The Speed of You We flesh bags consume/produce audio in “real-time”, aka a human clock rate .
Our neurons can only fire so fast. For a real-time conferencing product like Google Meet, latency needs to be near zero.
Any delay is super fucking annoying, which is why WebRTC does everything in its power to minimize it. Blocking on retransmissions will cause delays.
It’s the fatal flaw with TCP and why WebRTC is UDP based in the first place.
And worse yet, retransmissions will cause a rapid burst of audio on recovery. This is a bad user experience .
Humans do not want to wait, then process a burst of audio at 10x speed.
WebRTC instead primarily* relies on human retransmissions . You: What is le … France? Me: 🔇 You: I said, what is le capital of France? * Before a WebRTC warrior flames me on LinkedIn, read the fix it fix it fix it section. Are we doomed to mediocrity? Clock That Solder Boy Of course not. Wake up old man , it’s not 2020 any longer.
The internet is no longer for our flabby lips. Our robot overlords produce/consume audio based on a silicon clock rate .
We shoved electricity into a rock and now it can read a library in minutes.
What a time to be alive. Voice agents can hear and speak audio faster than real-time. Listening at 20x the speed? No problem. Speaking at 20x the speed? No problem. Humans stuck at real-time. We speak too slowly, so speech-to-text has to wait for us. We hear too slowly, so text-to-speech has to wait for us. WebRTC is designed for humans, not voice AI agents.
These poor robots are being held back by our mediocrity. I Require Context When it comes to LLMs, latency budgets get weird . Normally you would think of latency as the amount of time it takes for a grunt to traverse a tin can.
However, LLMs are blocked on context . i require context Here’s a dumb example of context growing over time: 1s : What 2s : What is 3s : What is le 4s : What is le capital 5s : What is le capital of 6s : What is le capital of France? If an LLM tries to answer my prompt before getting the full context, shit will suck. France is le gatekeeper , and everything before it is effectively a prerequisite.
In this example, what matters is the latency of the last packet . Those poor packets that were attacken by the kraken?
WebRTC actually had seconds to retransmit with no latency penalty.
The AI agent can process faster than real-time to catch up without the end user (aka YOU ) noticing a thing. So that’s what Mr. MoQ does.
No packet left behind: we keep retransmitting until the AI actually needs the audio. MoQ retransmits for up to 5s NET What is le capital of France? What is le capital of France? What is le capital of France? What is le capital of France? “Paris.” ▶ spoken / understood received, not yet understood waiting for retransmit get stuffed mr kraken It’s not expensive either: audio is tiny .
1s of Opus @ 64Kbps is 8KB, originally sent as 50 tiny packets, but it can be retransmitted as ~6 QUIC packets.
We have literal seconds to retransmit 6 packets to avoid any user impact. And if we manage to accomplish this herculean task: all the context arrives in time! The model no longer has to guess.
It no longer has to be trained on silence or distortion either. This is a pure user experience win . Not Just Mics Guess what?
WebRTC doesn’t just suck for STT, it also sucks for TTS. cars suck too, I’m an equal opportunity hater Fun Fact : WebRTC renders audio (and video) based on when it arrives , not when it is supposed to be rendered .
Every other protocol uses timestamps, but Mr. WebRTC barely looks at them, because accuracy is a non-goal.
Sure, it’ll nudge audio and video into sync by a few milliseconds, but good luck sending the video 500ms after the audio. This is a huge problem for voice AI .
TTS is generated faster than real-time, stamping each packet with a future timestamp.
But in order to play back audio at the correct time with WebRTC… the agent needs to sleep before transmitting each packet . And if there’s any packet loss, our TTS is lost, will never be retransmitted, tokens burned, yada yada. WebRTC sends at human speed, gives up on late audio NET Paris. Home of le croissant. Paris. Home of le croissant. Paris. Home of le croissant. Paris. Home of le croissant. “Sorry, you cut out. Home of what?” ▶ sent / played generated / buffered lost forever When the kraken attacken, there’s no coming backen. If only there was some way to signal when to render each audio packet.
A stamp of sorts. Random Access Memory Welcome back to the future Marty .
We faster than real-time now. RAM has this amazing property of being stupidly expensive.
And being able to store stuff locally.
You know, like audio that needs to be played over the speakers. We put a timestamp on each audio frame and use that to determine when to play it out of RAM.
Absurd, I know. MoQ sends everything ASAP, the player buffers NET Paris. Home of le croissant. Paris. Home of le croissant. Paris. Home of le croissant. Paris. Home of le croissant. “Huh, I didn’t know that.” ▶ sent / played generated / buffered waiting for retransmit I’m fast as fuck boye It’s how the Youtubes keeps playing back video even when you lose network connectivity.
MoQ does the same thing but for voice AI.
Your sick baking recipe won’t be subject to surprise congestion. And don’t you fret, 2 minutes of audio is only 1MB.
You’re not going to have to take out a loan to buy another RAM stick. Disclaimer : this behavior is not IETF standardized.
It’s something only my moq.dev clients (and thus Pipecat) support.
Be my guest if you want to argue with Cisco and get it into the official standards. Enter the Antagonist Then why is OpenAI using WebRTC ? WebRTC is the state of the art for real-time, conversational audio.
It’s available in every browser via libwebrtc , a C++ monolith maintained by Google.
It’s so complicated and sophisticated that Safari and Firefox use libwebrtc too, rather than vibe code their own like everything else.

abstract:
Genie 4 is now available Nov 18, 2026 | Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. Diego Rivas Group Product Manager, Google DeepMind Pavan Kumar Group Product Manager, Google Labs Read AI-generated summary We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers for creating interactive worlds. You can now modify environments in real time using text prompts and native audio features. Our updated Genie 3 model supports longer sessions, panorama grounding, and linked world sequences today. The new Project Genie agent helps you build custom worlds through simple natural language conversations. You can publish your creations to our community gallery for others to explore and remix. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are updating Project Genie to help you create and explore interactive digital worlds. With our new Genie 4 model, you can change weather, add characters, and hear adaptive audio in real time just by typing prompts. You can also use our new creative agent to build complex environments through simple conversation. If you subscribe to Google AI Ultra, you can start building, sharing, and remixing these custom worlds in our community gallery today. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. Experience Genie 4 in Project Genie With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. Discover new Genie 3 capabilities While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Extended sessions and world chaining: Explore for up to 3 minutes per generation (up from 60 seconds), or link multiple worlds together for longer journeys. 360-degree panorama image grounding: Seed new worlds from 360-degree panorama images. Real-time in-world events: Dynamically change the environment with natural-language prompts while you explore. Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command. Create new interactive experiences The new Project Genie agent takes creation beyond a single text or image prompt. Now crafting an interactive universe is as effortless as having a conversation. Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood. You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds. Turns a natural language prompt into an interactive spacewalk, then an alien spaceship appears on command Remix a hillside cafe into a glass pavilion in the desert. Publish custom worlds to the gallery for others to explore and remix. Explore the new gallery When you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. Transform personal photos into explorable spaces in “Living Memory,” wander through rich prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas in “Dino Field Guide,” or pit themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini serving as your real-time referee in “Rock Paper Scissors.” Browse curated and community-built worlds and jump straight into exploring. “Villa Giallo,” created with Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, uses Genie 4 to turn a gothic manor into an interactive, room-by-room mystery. “The Life of Ants,” built with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, uses Genie 4’s photorealism to let you navigate a colony from an ant’s perspective. The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism. Beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix. Learn how we are building responsibly We are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings. Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. For a deeper look into model limitations and our progress on these fronts, read our Genie 4 model research overview .
